Status
Guard installation. No civil administration of consequence
Population
not published. Throughput is
Principal exports

Guard installation world. Basic training.

Recorded training throughput, GC 4461: 141,880 entrants, 128,204 completions.

The intake returns are filed by name, age, parent world and prior status. They are among the most complete civil records in this archive, and they are not civil records.

Astonia INTACT
System
Astonia (single star, five bodies, one habitable)
Status
Guard territory. Annexed GC 4419
Population
between 60 million and 300 million
Membership
determined externally, by the annexation instrument, and not locally variable
Calendars in use
Galactic Calendar. The prior local reckoning is attested in testimony and has not been recovered
Principal exports
industrial diamond, milk, conscripted personnel

The sun does not rise here and does not set. It sits low on the rim of the sky and stays there, and the sky holds pink and yellow at every hour, over sand the colour of brass.

The dry ocean

There was a sea here for most of the world's history. Terraforming and drift took it away across about four hundred years, and the reefs it left are still standing. They stand where shrubs would stand on any other world: eight metres of coral in the open air, dry, pink and orange and a blue that carries after dark.

They do not grow. They do not rot either. There is enough water in the sand to hold them exactly as they are.

The people keep them alive. Households keep a spray bottle by the door and mist the formation nearest them, daily, everywhere in the settled belt. No ordinance requires it. We asked four informants why and got four answers, none of which was the same as another.

Diamond

The mountains are diamondiferous to a depth nobody has bothered to measure, which makes the stone here an industrial material and not a precious one. It goes out by the shipload for cutting tools. Children are given the flawed ones.

The night

The day is too hot to work in, so nothing happens in it. Trade, worship, school and every kind of public life happen after dark, under signage that runs pink and green above streets already lit like a long evening. This is a choice their grandparents made and not a fact of their bodies, and they will tell you so.

The bodies

Two Guard medical surveys, both dated GC 4416, record what everyone here already knew: Astonians are stronger than the human mean and harder to make ill. The first credits the milk, which comes from herds that graze on a forage that grows nowhere else. The second credits a lifetime spent breathing over the reefs, and lists eleven diseases the rest of the galaxy has no vaccine for and Astonians largely shrug off.

Both surveys recommend further study. No further study was undertaken.

The annexation instrument is dated GC 4419.

Schooling

After the annexation, the schools were handed to sponsored religious foundations on contract. The contracts survive and are specific: residential attendance, and instruction in Galactic Standard. Within eleven years they had 94 per cent of the children.

Levy

Astonians do not enlist. They are levied, under a clause of the same instrument. Yield for GC 4461: 41,208 persons. Royalty paid to the Royal houses that year on the same clause: 2,472,480 credits.

Worked moon of the Polaris system. Cold storage and freight.

Orbital rings and surface warehousing. Filed capacity: 411,000,000 tonnes under refrigeration.

Baline holds the system's stock between harvest and sale and is therefore the point at which the system's food is a commodity rather than a crop. The registrar records no third-generation residents.

The Burial Moon INTACT
Status
Guard establishment
Population
a caretaker establishment of 411
Principal exports
none

Grass to the horizon, a few footpaths, and small chapels at intervals. Nobody lives here except the people who cut the grass.

What it costs

In a galaxy of small crowded worlds, this is an entire moon given to the dead. That is the whole point and it is not sentimental: the annual maintenance appropriation is 8,204,600 credits and it has been granted in full every year since the establishment.

The numbers

Interred to date: 2,140,880. Surveyed and unallocated: 9,411,000.

How you get here

You wrote it down when you signed. Every person entering Guard service records their rites at enrolment: cremation or interment, faith or none, next of kin. A standard plot costs nothing. A custom monument, a custom plot, or more than two family members attending are chargeable, and the schedule of charges is filed.

Which means that somewhere there is a form where an eighteen-year-old ticked a box about their own body, and the Guard has kept it, and will honour it.

When it does not work

The establishment is built for individual services. There is one paragraph permitting a combined service at the caretakers' discretion when the numbers exceed what the moon can hold.

It has been used. The return for its use records attendance as a figure and the number of people commemorated as a range.

Corr INTACT

the R is rolled, here and in the shipping calls

System
Polaris
Status
licensed from Kelton. Local council retained, with limited competence
Population
between 600,000 and 5 million
Calendars in use
Polaris Harvest Reckoning
Principal exports
water

Ice and deep water, and a fleet of 2,206 tankers that runs it out to everybody else.

Kelton sets the allocation once a year, against the planting forecast for Weton and Tspa.

Which means the allocation is set before the planting, and therefore decides it. No instrument anywhere describes this as a power. Nothing in the system's constitution mentions it. It is simply what happens when one moon has the water and another moon has the fields.

Creta INTACT
System
Creta (single star, nine bodies, one habitable, three worked)
Status
independent. Observer standing with the Guard by treaty
Population
between 400 million and 1.2 billion
Membership
open, on assimilation. Ten years resident, fluent, and the continental civil code adopted entire
Calendars in use
Galactic Calendar; four continental reckonings, all agricultural, all within eleven days of one another
Principal exports
banking, insurance, arbitration, luxury manufacture, livestock, wine

Green mountains, lakes you can see the bottom of, and spring that does not end. Four continents, four governments, and more money than any of them will discuss.

Four countries, one policy

The continents govern themselves and have agreed on foreign policy by permanent convention, renewed without amendment forty-one times. What they argue about instead, in the record and in public, is fishing quota, water rights, and the correct preparation of two dishes.

Neutral, and armed about it

Creta was not invaded, not blockaded and not bombarded, through the entire war. Its own account credits universal service sized to make occupation expensive, and a standing refusal of basing rights to anybody.

Both belligerents also banked here throughout. We record that as a second fact and not as a correction to the first.

Service is eleven months and universal. The force has no long-range transport, no expeditionary doctrine, and no legal power to acquire either.

The vaults

Cretan deposit records survived the Wipe because they were on paper in rooms built to survive things. The four governments state that they are complete. They are not open to this archive, to the Guard, or to anyone else. Applications are answered promptly and in the negative.

The giving

Endowment records are public and precise. Between GC 4403 and 4462 Cretan foundations paid for 1,206 libraries, 411 hospitals and 89 university faculties on other worlds. Where the underlying capital came from is not published.

[Compiler's note: this society works from three rooms. Two of them were paid for by a Cretan endowment. We record that here because it seemed dishonest not to.]

The mills. Grain arrives raw from Weton and leaves as flour, oil and cake, and the difference between those two states is where the money in this system is made.

Throughput, GC 4461

1,188,400,000 tonnes in. 1,141,220,000 tonnes of finished product out.

The processing margin is the largest single margin in the system. It is realised on Kelton, where the product is sold, and not here, where it is made.

Dorrow has the second-highest output value of the ten inhabited bodies and the second-lowest household income.

    Katanzaria CONTESTED
    System
    Katanzaria (single star, six bodies, one habitable, one worked)
    Status
    independent. Trade agreement with the Guard, renewed six-yearly
    Population
    between 300 million and 1.4 billion
    Membership
    lineage. You may live here without it and it will get you nothing
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar for trade; the Katanzarian reckoning, which counts from a foundation we have not been able to fix against any other calendar
    Principal exports
    stone, worked metal, wine, oil, preserves, ritual craft

    Stone terraces, long tables, wine, and a monumental architecture raised on foundations nobody here laid. Governed by chieftains. Insists, officially and generally, that its people did not come from Wake.

    The disagreement

    Katanzaria holds that its people grew here and are related to nobody. The pre-war genetic surveys we hold in summary place them inside the human range with no distinguishing marker at all. Both are printed. They cannot both be right.

    There is a complication, and it is not a resolution. Katanzaria does have ruins older than its settlement, built in a way its own masons did not use and cannot copy, and a great deal of what stands here stands on them. That the ruins are not human is established. That the people are not human is not.

    Honour, which is not a decoration

    What is said about you after you die is the working currency of public life here, and the world's institutions are shaped around that. Katanzaria keeps the most complete civil registry in this archive, running eleven centuries, because a name is an asset and assets are recorded.

    Succession

    Chieftains, not kings. A title passes within a family but not by birth order: a brother, a cousin or a nephew may take it, and the recorded test is whether the family will be provided for. Alongside the martial component there is an electoral one, and titles have demonstrably moved by each.

    Duelling

    Recognised in statute, restricted by it, and much rarer in the record than in conversation. Twenty-two registered in the last century. Informants describe considerably more.

    Kelton INTACT
    System
    Polaris
    Status
    Guard administration. Seat of the harvest ledger, the licensing authority and the port
    Population
    between 8 million and 40 million
    Membership
    appointment or licence. Residence in the city requires one or the other
    Calendars in use
    Polaris Harvest Reckoning; Galactic for external contract
    Principal exports
    guarantees

    One city on the whole world, and beyond it small towns and a great deal of empty ground. Nothing edible is produced here.

    What the city makes is the promise that a harvest will be bought, stored, insured and delivered, and the paperwork that makes the promise enforceable. The exchange, the seed registry, the water allocation office, the quarantine authority, forty-one embassies and every insurer writing agricultural risk in the system are all inside it.

    Crop laboratories

    1,188 registered variant lines, developed here rather than on the worlds that grow them. Licence revenue for GC 4461: 96,440,200 credits.

    The arrangement

    A farmer on Weton may plant what she likes, harvest it, and sell it. Water, seed, storage, milling, shipping and sale each require an instrument issued in this city.

    Kitalia INTACT
    System
    Kitalia (single star, four bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    Guard member state. Acceded GC 4424 by referendum
    Population
    between 200 million and 800 million
    Membership
    residence, rate, and a name on a platform roll
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the Kitalian tide reckoning, twelve periods, still used in shipping and in law
    Principal exports
    marine protein, structural engineering, deep-foundation contracting

    They saw the water coming and they built above it. Pylons driven two kilometres to the seabed, and cities standing on top of them, and no land in use anywhere on the world.

    The engineering

    A glacial melt they could see coming two centuries out, and an answer that worked. This is the most completely documented infrastructure in the archive, because the works were financed from offworld and the financiers wanted certification at every stage: seabed surveys, weld schedules, inspection intervals, unit costs, all of it.

    Foundations run 1,180 to 2,340 metres. Design load 4.1 million tonnes. Certified to 260 knots sustained. They are, by every measure we can apply, magnificent.

    Living on one

    Dense and vertical, because there is no outward. The platform is the civic unit: your roll, your rate, your school, your council. There is no countryside and no farming of any consequence, and the whole arrangement rests on the assumption that the structure holds.

    Population by platform

    Not filed anywhere. Each platform kept its own roll, on itself.

    Burial

    There is no ground. What Kitalians do instead is done over water, and is catalogued separately.

    Maldo INTACT
    System
    Maldo (single star, eleven bodies, two habitable)
    Status
    Royal. Administrative capital
    Population
    between 90 million and 400 million
    Membership
    residence and registration. Office is open to any registered resident of five years
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the court calendar; the old foundry reckoning, which survives in guild documents and in the names of four public holidays
    Principal exports
    administration, arbitration, archives, antiques. Nothing is made here now

    They did not build the capital on a beautiful world. They built it on a used-up one, out of the used-up world itself, and every ministry and monument here is made of the ground it stands on.

    Five lives

    An ordinary green world. Then ore, and a boom. Then a century of heavy industry that made the surface uninhabitable and the sky a colour people still describe. Then the ore ran out and everyone left. Then the crown arrived, because a ruin is free land and the material was already lying on site.

    The city

    Built in a documented order, and the building registers survive complete for all sixty-one years of it: capital, then parliament, then monuments, then embassies, then houses spreading outward from all four. 3,308 principal structures.

    The catch

    All of it is Maldo steel, and there is no more Maldo steel. The ore body is worked out. Every repair to a Royal building anywhere is made in some other alloy, and the maintenance returns record the difference, structure by structure, as a falling percentage of original material.

    Now

    Population has fallen in each of the last four decennial returns. Working-age people leave; pensioners arrive. The largest single category of registered business on the world is the sale of antiques and reproductions to visitors.

    The capital of a monarchy is a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from.

    Marfeld INTACT
    System
    Marfeld (single star, eight bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    Guard member state
    Population
    between 30 million and 200 million
    Membership
    ritual. There is one route and no exemption, including for people born here
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the Marfeld reckoning, which has two seasons, hot and cold, and no word for anything between them
    Principal exports
    soldiers, hides, worked bone, draught animals

    A world that never lost its big animals. Everywhere else hunted them out. Here they are still in the country, in numbers, and everything about how people live on Marfeld follows from that one fact.

    Weather

    Two months of heat that kills, two months of cold that kills, and the turn between them comes fast enough that people plan for it the way other worlds plan for a storm. Nothing grows reliably. The diet was a hunting diet for most of the world's history and the cooking still tastes like one.

    Why the towns are the size they are

    A settlement here has to be big enough to wall and small enough to move, because the predators come through on the season and a wall is a delay, not an answer. No town on Marfeld has ever exceeded forty thousand people. No city has ever existed. Nobody local finds this remarkable.

    What they sell

    Marfeld sells men. They appear in the muster rolls of every army in the surviving record, in every period, listed by name and settlement and rate of pay, because Marfeld has kept that book for eleven centuries and keeps it still. They are contracted as professionals and paid as professionals, and the world is quite clear that this is a trade and not a tragedy.

    Guard recruiters have had a permanent office here since GC 4409. That is three years after the Guard existed and twenty-two before Marfeld joined it.

    The bombing

    Three times. The first took out the surface of half the northern continent during the war, and no target assessment held by this archive lists Marfeld in that sector at all. The second and third are catalogued as incidental to fighting between other parties.

    Casualty figures for all three exist and disagree with one another by a factor of ten.

    They rebuilt each time. Their own account of it is not grief and not defiance. It is closer to the way another world would talk about a bad winter.

    [Compiler's note: we asked forty-one men from this world to describe the trial. Every one of them declined. Two apologised.]

    System
    Maspin (single star, twelve bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    independent. Trailblazer port concessions in force. Royal tax jurisdiction asserted, and paid
    Population
    between 40 million and 200 million
    Membership
    the Council says there is no such thing, the people being one family
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar in the ports; the Maspin reckoning, anchored to the Season of Long Nights
    Principal exports
    flavoured fruits, kraskor, flooms

    Jungle to the horizon in every direction, and under it an ocean nobody has seen. Far enough out that most of the people born here will never leave, and poor enough that most of the ones who could, do not.

    The ground moves

    Eruption, quake, storm and flood are annual here rather than exceptional. The Council's own submissions to the Royal treasury, which we hold in copy, list within one nine-year stretch: four eruptions, eleven significant quakes, two monasteries lost to water, and burned crop across an area the submission does not put a number to.

    The fruit

    Remote worlds cannot sell bulk, so Maspin sells what only Maspin has. The fruit here comes in flavours that do not occur elsewhere and it travels badly, which is precisely why the offworld rich pay what they pay for it. Everything else the world exports is an animal or a plant that also grows somewhere closer.

    The ocean underneath

    The Maspin hold that the water beneath the crust is alive, that they are made from it, and that they go back into it. They do not present this as belief. They present it as the way the world is put together, in the tone another people would use for the tides.

    Survey material confirms a large subsurface body of water. It says nothing else at all.

    What it costs to be here

    Maspin remits to the Royal houses, and the figure is filed to the credit: 10,000,000 royal credits in the most recent solar rotation returned.

    Against that we can set no disbursement, no relief, and no acknowledgement of receipt. The Council's file records fourteen requests for assistance across nineteen years. We hold no reply to any of them, and the Council says none came.

    Labour

    Maspin calls itself a slave-free territory, and the declaration is accurate as the law defines the word. Indenture is lawful here and is administered by the Council itself.

    Modanick INTACT
    System
    Modanick (single star, four bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    Guard member state. Acceded GC 4427 by referendum, 71.4 per cent for, on a turnout of 88.2
    Population
    between 200 million and 900 million
    Membership
    descent. Anyone may live here. Municipal office is restricted by statute to people born in the municipality
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar for filings; the Modanick reckoning, four seasons anchored to first frost, for everything anyone actually says out loud
    Principal exports
    physicians, surgical instruments, pharmaceuticals, tuition, cheese, cut flowers

    Cold, close-built and comfortable. Brick, iron gates, chimneys, canals that freeze hard enough to skate by the second week. The kind of world that produces doctors and cheese and very little history.

    Winter

    Four months of it, and it is not violent. It is an inch a day, most days, for a third of the year. The canals go over and stay over, the skating leagues run, and the national game is played on them by people who learned it before they could read.

    Nothing on this world is more than nine storeys, by municipal code, in every municipality, each of which passed the code separately.

    Flowers

    Spring here is a serious business. Botany is a national art rather than a hobby, the flower shows are old and formal, and the shortest route to being taken seriously in a Modanick town is to be good at growing something.

    Why the doctors

    Crowding plus long winters made this a plague world for six generations. Hospital foundation dates cluster tightly in that period, and so does the local expectation, still written into the school statutes, that a person be fully formed by twenty. The plagues stopped. The expectation did not.

    The world now supplies more trained physicians to the member worlds than any other, and manufactures no weapons at all.

    Defence

    None. Modanick has never had a military. Its accession instrument settles the personnel obligation in cash, one of four such instruments in the register: it pays 3.9 per cent of member revenue and sends nobody.

    A note on the weather

    Guard tourism material issued between GC 4440 and GC 4455 describes Modanick as warm and bright the year round. The municipal weather returns for the same years describe something else. We hold the returns.

    Monver INTACT
    System
    Monver (single star, five bodies, one habitable, one worked)
    Status
    Guard member state. Acceded GC 4431 on negotiated terms
    Population
    between 80 million and 350 million
    Membership
    two years of service, and you do not tell us how to live
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the Monver reckoning, six seasons, anchored to the high thaw
    Principal exports
    people, timber, engineering trades, regulated botanicals

    Forest, rock and real mountains, some of which are ships. Colonial hulls came down here two thousand years ago and the country grew over them, and the largest is thirty-one kilometres long and carries mature trees.

    The bargain

    Monver's accession instrument is the most heavily qualified in the member register. It reserves local government, local statute on botanicals, and every local observance, each by name. In exchange it gives two years of everybody.

    Most of that service is a trade school with a rifle in it. The certificates issued under it are good across the member worlds and a Monveri carpenter is a Monveri carpenter anywhere.

    What it costs them

    Monver holds about 0.9 per cent of the member population and supplies 4.1 per cent of member personnel, and has done every year since it joined. They are proud of this and say so.

    The permissiveness

    Redleaf is lawful here and taxed like anything else. The line, given to us more or less identically by nine people, is that men who fight hard should be allowed to relax hard, and that it helps with what fighting does to you. Mostly that is true.

    The health returns record, annually, a minority for whom it is not recreation any more. No local statute addresses them. No local politician has proposed one. It is the only subject on this world where a straight question gets a change of topic.

    The Force

    2 gaps

    Monver kept its Planetary Defence Force under the accession terms and did not dissolve it. Monveri units fought at [...] before the merger. [RECORD DAMAGED]

    Nhathar INFERRED
    System
    not fixed in any schedule we hold
    Status
    not filed. No accession, no protectorate, no occupation order
    Population
    not established
    Calendars in use
    lunar. Nothing further recovered
    Principal exports
    contracted personnel

    The Nhath homeworld. Hot, dry, volcanic, and almost everything anyone knows about it has been reconstructed from the language rather than from a visit.

    What the language says about the place

    Nhathian has two weather words, rain and wind, and no others, which is a vocabulary you get on a world with two things the sky does. It has a dedicated word for creatures regarded as food. Its numbers run in base eight because Nhath hands have four fingers, and that follows the whole way down: tools cut for a four-finger grip, eight-sided rooms, days divided into eight-hour blocks, and fighting formations of eight.

    Their word for the sun is short and hard. Their word for the moon is long and flowing. Sun means exposure. The moon is sacred, and raids are timed to it.

    Black rock and lava

    Outside accounts of the surface are few and consistent: volcanic country, dark stone, heat coming off the ground, and settlements built low.

    The Guard's contracts with Nhath parties identify them by job code. They do not record where they came from.

    Polaris INTACT

    the star. On several outer settlements an older common word for the sun remains in use

    Primary of the agricultural system that supplies the greater part of the member worlds' staple grain, protein, and salt.

    Type and survey data

    filed complete in the navigational schedules, re-surveyed GC 4431.

    Name

    The star's name is older than its use. A family took the name from the star. Approximately a millennium later that family became royal, and the name is now borne by a Royal house, by the star, by the system, and by the shared calendar of ten inhabited bodies.

    Consequently no resident of the system can name the star that grows their food without naming the house that holds the licence on it. Certain outer settlements retain a prior common word for the sun in daily speech. It appears in no filing, no contract, and no ledger, and the Restoration has been told by three separate informants that it is not used in front of buyers.

    The Polaris System INTACT

    also known as: the breadbasket

    Composition
    two planets, Kelton and Weton, and eight worked moons
    Status
    Guard administration seated on Kelton. Outer bodies keep local government. Licensing, banking and the harvest ledger do not
    Population
    between 200 million and 900 million across all ten
    Membership
    application, and assessment. There are more applicants than places in every year returned
    Calendars in use
    the Polaris Harvest Reckoning, shared across all ten because the logistics demand it. Galactic Calendar for external contracts only
    Principal exports
    grain, flour, oil, protein, meat, salt, seed, drink

    Ten inhabited bodies running one machine with the parts on separate worlds. Most of what the member worlds eat comes out of here.

    How it fits together

    Weton grows the grain. Dorrow mills it. Sheel raises the meat and, out of the same yards, renders the bone and blood the Weton soil runs on. Corr ships the water. Schriggé ships the salt. Tspa grows the protein. Tall holds the seed. Baline holds the cold. Kelton holds the paperwork.

    Break any one of those and the system stops. Most people in it can name three.

    What you get

    A house, a guaranteed price for your crop, a wage floor, a rest day, and a repair entitlement that means when the combine breaks it gets fixed. We have compared these terms against forty-one other agricultural worlds. Nothing comes close. Farmers move here on purpose, and apply, and wait.

    Clause 11

    Leaving the system requires an approved leave filing that states a date of return. It sits at clause eleven of the standard residence instrument and the port authority on Kelton enforces it. Filings are approved 96.8 per cent of the time.

    The scrip

    Wages are paid in Polaris scrip, which is excellent money and is not money anywhere else. Conversion to Guard credits happens at the Kelton exchange, subject to an annual per-person limit that 0.4 per cent of holders reach.

    You can leave. You cannot take it with you.

    The libraries

    Funded from the harvest levy and unusually good: a mean of 41,000 volumes a settlement against a member-world mean of 9,200. A great deal of it is about economics, which is to say about yield, supply, and the dignity of feeding people.

    [Compiler's note: nothing is banned here. We checked. There is simply no line in the acquisitions schedule for it.]

    Dust, a river, a clock tower and a fuel depot. Occupied because of where it is and for no other reason anyone has written down.

    Position, and nothing else

    Resmole sits on the shortest surveyed lane between two sectors that matter, and it has one river, one usable plain, and enough flat ground for airstrips. The basing schedule lists a shipport, two strips, a fuel depot and a transit function. It lists no other purpose, because there is no other purpose.

    The civil programme

    Chartered on occupation and funded for four years. Its final report is held. Every appropriation after that is nil.

    The fighting

    Continuous and low-intensity, for long enough that nobody flinches. Local combatants work out of a tunnel network that appears on no map in this archive. Garrison casualties run eleven to nineteen a year and are filed by name.

    Local casualties are not filed at all.

    System
    Saigo (single star, six bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    Guard member state and chartered university world
    Population
    between 50 million and 250 million
    Membership
    residence and rate. Matriculation confers residence
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the term calendar, which governs everything here including the shipping
    Principal exports
    engineers, patents, instruments, research

    Warm, coastal, and organised entirely around a university. It is the place trying to rebuild the machines that stopped in GC 4401, and it is losing, slowly, in public.

    The programme

    Every drone, remote and unmanned system in the galaxy died at once and none of them came back. The reconstruction was chartered here in GC 4412 and has been funded ever since. Output to date: 2,411 registered patents and eleven classes of working device.

    What people think of that

    The member consultations are consistent and they contradict themselves. Asked whether autonomous systems should be rebuilt, respondents say no by a wide margin. Asked separately what they miss most about the world before, they say those systems.

    Both answers are in the same returns, from the same people, in the same year.

    Character

    There is no industry here that is not attached to the university and no politics that is not conducted inside it. The beaches are good and the students use them.

    A religious note

    What this volume catalogues as Simulationism is concentrated here and is professed disproportionately among senior faculty and the donors who fund them. Saigo does not treat this as a religious matter and files no observance for it.

    Sansvor CONTESTED

    said quickly by anyone from there, the name comes out in about a syllable and a half

    System
    Sansvor (single star, ten bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    independent. No garrison. Guard consulate since GC 4433
    Population
    between 100 million and 600 million
    Membership
    residence. There is no instrument and no authority empowered to issue one
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar in the ports; at least four local reckonings in daily use, none official
    Principal exports
    none of consequence. Scholarship, salvage, and people

    A rich world that stopped being maintained. Almost nothing here was destroyed. Almost nothing here has been repaired either, and the difference between those two sentences is the whole of the place.

    What they built

    The century before the war was an inventive one here and they spent it: airship terminals, rail, cut stone, cathedrals, civic halls, libraries with reading rooms sixty metres long. Then the paint ran out, and nobody made more paint, and a wall came down and there were no stonecutters left.

    The characteristic building on Sansvor is structurally sound and open to the sky.

    Why that is survivable

    The weather is mild. A classroom missing a wall and half a ceiling is still a classroom here, and is used as one. Desks, board, books, and you keep your coat on. Birds come in. Nobody stops the lesson.

    Nothing in the country is dangerous. Prey animals, and a raptor that takes them.

    Who is still here

    The universities did not close. Their endowments failed, the faculties went unpaid, and a good number of them kept teaching anyway. Literacy returns, where a local authority still bothers to produce one, are among the highest in this archive. The museums are intact and uncatalogued. Dragon's blood trees have come up through the roof of the north rail terminal and are now part of the roof.

    Politics

    1 gap

    Between nineteen and thirty organised associations of any weight, the range being a disagreement about what counts. Read their literature and you find the argument is about what the world used to be and who gets to say what it becomes next. It is not about food. Nobody here is short of food.

    The blockade, and the reason this entry is filed as contested.

    Guard material, and most people in the port towns, hold that a belligerent closed the world's shipping during the war and the Guard broke it open in GC 4409, and that the Guard is therefore remembered here as the people who came.

    A smaller number, mostly inland, hold that the closing continued after the war ended, and continued deliberately, until the world could be relied on to ask.

    Port manifests would settle it. The port record for GC 4402 to 4409 is not in this archive. [FILING INCOMPLETE]

    Shayron INTACT
    System
    Shayron (single star, seven bodies, one habitable)
    Status
    Royal. Ceremonial seat
    Population
    between 20 million and 110 million
    Membership
    residence, and the municipal rate. There has never been another requirement
    Calendars in use
    Galactic Calendar; the Shayron liturgical calendar, filed with nobody, surviving in the observance of registered scholars
    Principal exports
    almost nothing. Chocolate, beer, hospitality, restoration work

    Jasmine, cut stone, and an afternoon that seems to last all day. No industry, no exhaust, and a city built in four eras stacked on top of each other, any of which you can reach by digging eleven metres in more or less any direction.

    Built to study religion

    Shayron had no natives and no founding stock. It was endowed as a place to think about faith: libraries, monastic houses, workshops, and scholars of any belief maintained without regard to which.

    What came out of that is the art. Faiths in competition commission better work than faiths at peace, and the mosaic and glass of the old quarters is the largest surviving body of pre-war craft anywhere, and the only one where the workshop, the commission and the payment are all still on file.

    Why it went quiet

    Scholars do not proselytise. Newer faiths spread around this world rather than through it. The monastic register records three centuries of decline and the formal closure of nine quarters, and there is no conquest in it, no plague, no disaster. Enrolment simply stops.

    Two of the nine were closed with a single person left inside, in both cases at that person's request.

    Why the crown could take it

    By agreement, and the instrument survives. The Royals were sympathetic to the old faith and wanted a seat that was beautiful, defensible and of no economic consequence whatsoever. The scholars wanted their foundations protected.

    Both got it. Registered scholars still hold exemption from the rate and from levy. The register of exempt persons has not been audited since GC 4361.

    Underneath

    The sewers of the earliest city still run under all of it, and are still in service, because nobody ever found a reason to replace something that works.

    Frozen through, dark almost all of the time, and lit from above by an aurora that does not stop. There is nothing here. That is the whole of its strategic value and the whole of its history.

    What it is for

    Sonaff appears in Guard planning as a waypoint and a place to leave things. It has no assessed resource value. Nobody has ever contested it because nobody has ever wanted it.

    Why it matters anyway

    Being worthless made it reachable. Missionary orders came here early and kept coming, and a number of the populations out on those moons, including populations that will not tolerate contact of any other kind, hold faiths that arrived from Sonaff.

    That is the most consequential thing about this moon and it appears in no official filing.

    Wake CONTESTED

    also known as: Waketin · the Wakeful Islands · Origin

    System
    Wake (single star, six bodies, one formerly habitable)
    Status
    destroyed. Licensed extraction zone under the Guard Board of Directors
    Population at loss
    somewhere between 900 million and 4 billion. The Restoration accepts no figure
    Membership
    [ENTRY NOT RECOVERED]
    Calendars in use
    none surviving
    Principal exports
    Corefuel

    A field of rock where a planet used to be. Held almost everywhere to be where humans came from, on the strength of genetic sampling whose method did not survive the people who used it.

    Before

    Every source we hold agrees it was a capital world. That is the only detail about this planet on which our sources do not disagree.

    There is no census material. No municipal roll, no tax register, no conscription list, no birth record, nothing. Several people have described the census offices to us by location. None of the buildings survive.

    The loss

    Guard records say one ordnance deployment, Autumnal forces, GC 4394, over in under an hour.

    Thirty-eight people across eleven settlements say it took between two and nine days. Six of them describe the sky changing colour before anything was heard. Four describe evacuation orders. One describes those orders being countermanded.

    We print both. They cannot both be correct.

    After

    Mantle and core in pieces, sixty-one of them dense enough to be worth working. The Corefuel comes out of those, and it comes out of nowhere else with a licence on it, and the licence is issued by the Guard Board of Directors alone.

    The ledgers for that trade are INTACT and unusually complete. Licensed extraction for GC 4461: 812,443.6 standard tonnes.

    People lived out there while it was worked. Houses on the larger fragments, held down and given air by spires burning the planet they were standing on. There was a school.

    Settlement names, populations and outcomes were not filed.

    [Compiler's note: we hold four hundred and eleven pages of extraction ledger for this world and one page of anything else.]

    Grain from one horizon to the other, worked by families on long instruments with machinery nobody can build any more.

    Harvest, GC 4461

    1,204,880,600 tonnes, of which 1,204,880,600 tonnes were bought at the scheduled price. The purchase guarantee has been met in every year on record.

    What Weton does not have

    Its soil comes from Sheel. Its water is allocated from Corr. Its seed is licensed from Tall. Its grain leaves raw and is milled on Dorrow. It holds none of those functions and has never asked for one.

    The machines

    Every combine and hauler here is pre-war and irreplaceable, kept running under the system repair entitlement by yards whose senior mechanics are the most consequential people in any given district. A farmer here can afford to fix the tractor. That is not true anywhere else in this archive and everybody here knows it.

    Wages are good. Wages are in scrip.

    Peoples

    11 entries 5 contested
    Astonians INTACT

    The people of a world with no sunrise, and the reason the Guard wanted it.

    They are stronger than the human mean and they are harder to make ill, and both of those were measured and written down three years before anybody annexed anything.

    Strength

    Bone density and muscle mass well above the range. Guard survey credits the milk, which comes from herds grazing a forage that grows nowhere else. It is not training and it is not selection. They are simply built that way, and they were built that way before the Guard arrived.

    Immunity

    A lifetime breathing over the dry reefs leaves them shrugging off eleven diseases nobody has a vaccine for.

    Both surveys recommended further study. Neither study happened. The annexation happened.

    Since

    Astonians do not enlist, they are levied, under a clause of the instrument. Forty-one thousand a year. Their failure rate at basic training is a third of the member-world average, which surprises nobody who has read the first half of this entry.

    The Dead Moon raiders TESTIMONY

    White cloaks in a whiteout, black masks with nothing on them but metal eyepieces, long rifles with bayonets fixed.

    Not a species. A faction, drawn from several populations of the cold outer moons, and beyond that nobody knows how it is put together. No structure, no leader, no territory, no demand has ever been recorded. They do not hold ground and do not appear to want any.

    Everybody who has survived contact says the same thing about the way they move, which is that they are in no hurry. They come out of the storm at a walk.

    The one thing that stops them

    Missionaries reached those moons out of Sonaff, and a number of raider populations hold the same faith as communities they are otherwise permanently at war with. There is at least one recorded case of a raider breaking off in the middle of an action on seeing a devotional pendant.

    Not surrender, not mercy, not law. A pendant.

    The Gashi INTACT

    Green-skinned, and nobody can agree on whether that skin is reptile or amphibian.

    Up close it settles the question no better. It has the fine dry grain of scale in some lights and the give of something that would rather be damp in others, and the Gashi themselves find the question tedious in the way any people find it tedious when strangers open with it.

    What they wear

    Robes and tunics, cut long, and over them a great deal of decorative gear that is built to move: panels, sashes, hanging lengths of fabric weighted at the ends so they swing and settle rather than hang dead. A Gashi walking across a room is doing something that a human walking across a room is not.

    The hair

    All colours, every variety, and no two families the same. What is consistent is the quality of it. Gashi hair grows thick, holds a shape, takes a comb, and looks in every case as though it has just been finished by somebody very good, which is not a thing they work at and is very annoying to everyone else.

    What they do

    Artisans, overwhelmingly, in the broad sense rather than the narrow one. Chefs, painters, teachers, engravers, people who make the small good version of a thing that could have been made badly and cheaply instead. It is a whole world, so it is also farmers and clerks and mechanics, but the culture is built around art and sophistication and it judges accordingly.

    Which makes the ones who go into other lines of work interesting, because the sophistication does not come off. It just gets applied to something else.

    Humans CONTESTED

    Four out of every five people alive. Present on every inhabited world in this volume except eleven.

    Where from

    Wake, by general account, on the strength of pre-war genetic sampling that we have the conclusions of and not the method. The technique is lost, so the finding cannot be checked, and at least one very populous world rejects it outright. That is why this entry is filed as contested and not because the question is genuinely open.

    Colour does not matter here

    Human populations vary continuously in colouring, height and feature, everywhere, and no world in this archive organises status around it. No statute anywhere in our holdings mentions it. Every planet is mixed and nobody thinks about it.

    What humans sort each other by instead is world, bloodline, profession and service, and those they enforce, sometimes at law. A Modanicker will not let you hold municipal office. Katanzaria will not give you standing without lineage. Marfeld will not call you a man until you have walked into the country alone.

    The word

    Crag, for anyone who is not human, is a human coinage in general human use, and it is universal for exactly the reason the first line of this entry gives. When four fifths of everyone is one thing, that thing stops noticing itself.

    The Maspin TESTIMONY

    Bodies of smoke and vapour, about the height of a human child. Where the eyes should be there is water, held somehow, and it moves. Inside the head there is an ember, and it brightens.

    They have no mouths. The voice arrives anyway, from somewhere further in.

    Faces

    The features shift with feeling, continuously, the way a fire does. Other peoples report that you learn to read this with practice and cannot read it at all before. Every human informant who has spent a season among them says the same thing: it is not that Maspin are hard to read, it is that they cannot stop being read.

    Sparks

    Snap the fingers and they come, enough to light a cigar. This is universal, nobody here finds it worth mentioning, and every visitor mentions it.

    Eating

    Mostly they do not. They take byproduct from the plants around them the way other people take oxygen, with rather more water vapour in it. What they do eat is liquid or close to it: fruit pulped and watered and drunk, absorbed into the smoke of the body rather than swallowed.

    Nothing in the diet is chewed. Everything is fermented, pickled, pulped or brewed.

    Family

    They have families, and the shape of one is not what other peoples mean by the word. Ask a Maspin who their family is and the answer takes in the household, the settlement, and eventually everybody, and they are not being poetic about it.

    Nobody outside has ever got further than that. Maspin is a long way out, most Maspin never leave it, and very few outsiders stay long enough to be told anything that is not a courtesy. What is known about how a Maspin household actually works is roughly what a visitor picks up in a season, which is not much, and everybody who has written about it has been a visitor.

    Dying

    They hold that they are made from the ocean under the crust and that they go back into it. What that looks like in practice is catalogued under the Elder Tree, and it is not a metaphor.

    Work

    Fruit, kraskor, floom husbandry, port labour, temple and civic service, and the professions. Among our informants were a chemist, a caretaker, a councillor, and a clerk who keeps the tide tables at Riflo port and asked us twice whether we needed anything else.

    Status

    Indenture is lawful on Maspin and is administered by the Council. A number of the people in this entry are serving one.

    The Nhath CONTESTED

    There are two Nhath in the surviving record and they are not the same people.

    The one in the invoices

    1 gap

    Guard contracting files, INTACT, complete in the way commercial files always are: scope, duration, rate, settlement. Eleven separate engagements across nineteen years. Paid in full and on the scheduled date, every time.

    The fund that paid them is identified by an internal reference. We have not established what it denotes. [FILING INCOMPLETE]

    Guard ministerial material describes the same people as raiders without political organisation.

    The one in the grammar

    Recovered language material, and it describes something else entirely. Verbs that conjugate by subject. Two levels of you, chosen by the status of the person you are addressing, where the wrong choice is not a rudeness. Numbers in base eight, named after the fingers, extending without limit. Colours that are all derived from things: red is blood-colour, white is clean-colour, silver is weapon-colour.

    And a genealogy. Every Nhath carries a generation number, counted in eights, inherited and incremented. The recovered examples run into three figures.

    A people with no political organisation does not keep an eighty-eight generation line. A people that keeps one is not described by an invoice.

    How they say themselves

    Their word for themselves is their word for we. Everyone else in the galaxy calls them by it, which means every world in this archive addresses them, without knowing it, as us.

    There is one word for everybody outside: krayd. It serves for they, for other species, and for enemy. The language provides nothing neutral for a stranger.

    Work

    Armed contract, which is what the Guard bought and therefore what the record shows. Also haulage, salvage, and the sale of water rights. The survey notes an instructor of arithmetic at a settlement school, by name and generation number, and records his rate of pay.

    Pre-human inhabitants of Wake TESTIMONY

    Something was on Wake before us, and it is buried in the mantle.

    That is legend, and we would not print it at all except for one thing: it is told, in recognisable form, by at least six populations that had no contact with each other before the war. Traditions that share nothing else share this.

    Where the versions agree

    That they were very old. That they reached a point where they no longer died. That this turned out not to be what they wanted. That they had a hand in making humans afterwards. And that something of theirs is still in us, described in every version as a fault rather than a gift.

    Where they disagree

    Everything else, including whether any of them is left.

    There is no artefact, no structure, no remains and no document. Ruins built by somebody nobody can identify do exist, on Katanzaria and elsewhere, which proves there were predecessors somewhere and proves nothing at all about these.

    Species of unresolved classification CONTESTED

    A family of peoples on the outer trade worlds where nobody can agree how many peoples it is.

    The problem

    One survey says a single species with extraordinary variation in body plan. Another says between four and nine separate species sharing a range.

    The evidence for one species is uncomfortable and strong. Marriage and inheritance records from three worlds show direct parentage between individuals who look nothing alike: in the best case a heavy grey ambulatory parent on several limbs and a hard-shelled offspring with a crab's mouth, recorded at the time by a port registrar who had no stake in the argument.

    Growing up

    The young of at least some of these lineages go through a long stretch where the body is awake and capable and responsive and there is nobody home behind it. It runs from a few years to more than a decade. It is not an illness and it is not a disability. It is a stage, and it ends.

    Why it matters legally

    Galactic Standard law assigns rights by species and requires that a species be named. Where nobody can name it, the code has no answer, and the practical outcome in the port registers is that these people hold whatever status the clerk on duty wrote down.

    [Compiler's note: the word catalogued elsewhere in this volume as crag covers every population in this entry with one syllable. People who use it in our hearing can usually tell nine kinds of grain apart by sight.]

    The Targath CONTESTED

    Blue gel inside a jagged shell, and one eye that goes all the way round the head and shows you everything at once. They take prey apart rather than killing it, and they are, by every account we have, fond of humans.

    A caution about this entry

    Every physical description we hold was taken in a prison yard or a custody suite. Nobody has surveyed a Targath settlement. We are describing a people entirely from the condition of the ones who have been caught.

    The web

    The account in circulation holds that a Targath construction beneath a planet's crust pulled a whole fleet and everybody in it to the ground, armour and weapons dragged down, with nobody left to report it.

    It comes from inside the Guard officer corps and it is repeated there. We can trace it to no document and no named witness, and we are obliged to point out that the claim nobody survived and the description of what happened come from the same mouth.

    The bombing

    Their jungle settlements were struck with second-generation Torkal aircraft. The sortie returns are INTACT: aircraft, crew, hours, ordnance loaded, ordnance released, grids struck, all filed.

    Population of those grids is not filed. No census of them was ever taken by anybody.

    Work

    Subsurface farming, mineral extraction, tunnelling under contract. And prison labour: Targath appear on the custodial rolls of two Guard installations at a proportion the population figures cannot account for, digging magnetic ore.

    The survey material also notes one Targath keeping accounts for a port concession, and records that the books were in order.

    The Vitula CONTESTED

    Two metres and more. Grey, and wet to the touch. Eight white eyes set around the head, so that there is no direction they cannot see. On the back, folded and useless, a pair of wings that have not carried anything in a very long time.

    The body

    Insect-descended, and without the shell you would expect from that: all of the mass is muscle and nerve. They breathe badly off their own worlds and wear masks everywhere else, bought by the employer and deducted from the wage.

    Pain registers in them below the human mean. That is a property of the nervous system, documented in the pre-war literature, and it means what it says: they feel it less, so they keep working.

    The disagreement

    Guard instructional material says the Vitula have a collective mind and no individual will. The surviving biology says pheromone signalling, proximity awareness, and a distress sense good to about 1.6 kilometres that carries no content beyond the fact that somebody is hurt.

    Both are printed here. They describe different animals.

    Work

    Excavation, tunnelling, deep foundation, haulage, foundry, and armed contract. Vitula crews appear in the construction record of eleven worlds, including as subcontractors on the Kitalia pylons, listed by crew and by rate. The kingdoms themselves are small, farmed at the surface and mined underneath.

    When a king or queen dies, the pattern in the record is not succession crisis and not reprisal. It is a cluster of new engagements. The crews go and find whoever is hiring. This has been observed four times.

    One further fact

    Guard field instruction includes anatomy for this people, specifying the location of the heart. The manual is INTACT, is in current issue, and places that lesson at the same point in the syllabus as the lesson on how to operate a weapon.

    Berji Keggit INTACT

    also: Kegan

    The tallest man on Castle Team by a clear head, and the least interested in acting like it.

    Blond hair, tightly curled, cut short. Green eyes at the far end of the range, the sort people comment on and he waves off. Broad through the shoulders and imposing out of armour right up until he moves, which he does with a loose, excited, faintly lanky energy that undoes the whole effect. Green visor.

    Monver

    Forested, mountainous, locally governed, extremely proud of itself, and deeply relaxed about what people do on their own time. He fought a war on his own ground with the Planetary Defence Force before he was ever Guard, on the side that won and then merged in.

    What he actually is

    A cook, a beach person, and a light and tasteful druggie. He does not believe in hierarchies and is not especially interested in ethics either. What moves him is his people: his friends, his family, and keeping them safe. He will do things he would rather not discuss to that end and will not pretend the cause had anything to do with it.

    He is engaged. She is a botanist with the Guard's scientific service, and what they have in common is growing things, cooking them, and smoking the ones that are for smoking.

    He does an impression of a Guard officer, at bars, at length, with a name he made up on the spot and has used ever since.

    He talks in stories rather than principles, and he is the one who says the thing that lands. You can't hate yourself into being better. And the old Monveri line about a ship in harbour being safe and belonging somewhere else entirely.

    His enlistment runs out shortly and he has not filed anything about extending it.

    Calsco Fritt CONTESTED

    Seven feet of Katanzarian in a fur hide, with cross-draw revolvers, tribal tattoos, and a laugh you can hear from the other end of a settlement.

    He runs the Trailblazer concession on Maspin: the port, the medbay, the flooms, the deal with the local council. He is very good at it, and he is good at it because he is a superb reader of people who has had a lot of practice.

    He negotiates with a floom tucked under one arm, stroking it absently while he talks, and the effect on the other side of the table is exactly what he intends it to be. Gold holowatch. Greyleaf, constantly.

    He is theatrical, manipulative, warm, and genuinely funny, usually all four inside one sentence. He lectures on politics entirely in metaphor, and when somebody asks him to drop the metaphors he is wounded about it and does it anyway, badly.

    He also butchers people's names on purpose, and waits to see whether they will correct him.

    Why he is out here

    He was a chieftain on Katanzaria and he is not one now. Three versions of how that happened circulate on his own world. One says he failed a ritual obligation. One says he lost a duel. The third says he was simply out-manoeuvred in the electoral half of the succession, which is lawful, carries no dishonour, and is the only one of the three that would leave no mark on a world that writes everything down.

    He would rather people believed either of the first two. Those happen in an arena.

    Home

    He is married, to a woman he describes as fierce and brilliant and beautiful, and he cannot go back to her without either a title or something heroic to his name. He is working on it.

    Cillus Vot Shayron-Skoln INTACT

    A prince of the blood who wanted to be a war correspondent, and got what he asked for.

    Ginger, a deep earthy orange rather than a bright one, shaved close at the sides with just enough length on top to curl. Clear skin. Tall and toned without being strong, and not thin either. His eyes read as big without actually being big, and that is the whole problem with his face: it announces, from across a landing pad, that nothing has ever happened to him.

    Softly spoken. Endearing before he has said anything worth being endeared by.

    He grew up behind castle walls on Shayron with everything arranged for him, and left specifically to find out what the galaxy actually looks like. What he found was worse than he had pictured.

    How a Royal ends up with a Guard squad

    The Royal forces and the Guard are close. They train together, exercise together, and lend each other people, in the way two friendly militaries always have. A Royal journalist embedded with Guard formations is unusual but not strange, and he volunteered for it expecting routine work: a few weeks with a line unit, some morale footage, a report home about ordinary business.

    He shoots footage of squads for exactly that purpose, and at one point he shoots Squad 412 celebrating with looted goods.

    What he wears

    A religious pendant, given rather than bought, and he does not take it off.

    The colony recovery detail RECOVERED

    The Guard element that walked the Corefuel colony after the raid, and the two men in it who matter.

    The soldier who lifted the floorboard

    He did it because it was the next board. He was not searching for anybody. That is the whole thing: a routine sweep of a burned house, done properly, by somebody who had no reason to expect anything under there.

    The officer

    He read the station chief off a scan, marked him killed in action, and closed the family out on an assumption spoken flatly enough that it was clearly not the first time he had said it.

    "There's probably not even a body left after those ion bombs."

    Daiser INTACT

    Caretaker of the Council's temple at Riflo, and the sharpest person in the building.

    He is introduced to offworlders as the Gatekeeper, which is what the job is called and not what he is. He opens the great oak doors, receives you, and shows you where to stand, and it is very easy to treat him as furniture for the first ten minutes.

    "He's not just a gatekeeper. His name is Daiser. He's... like you. Someone surviving the pressure. Don't add more weight to his shoulders."

    A Maspin: smoke and vapour, water where the eyes should be, an ember behind it all that brightens when he is enjoying himself, which is often.

    The situation

    He is indentured. Sentenced to work off a debt that exists on paper and nowhere else, with seven years still on it and no wage to buy it out with. His holder is an establishment controlled by his own uncle, who sits on the Council. Everybody involved regards this as normal, including, most of the time, Daiser.

    "We call it indentured servitude. Where I work off an imaginary debt until I can pay it off and be free, which is actually fucking hard without a paycheck."

    Before that

    A chemist, and a properly trained one. He can make things most people cannot get, including weapons that are banned on his own world.

    How he talks

    Two registers, switched instantly. Street with anyone he likes. An elaborate, over-polished formal voice for anyone with authority, deployed with a completely straight face, which is its own kind of insult.

    He has never flown. He has never been off Maspin at all.He has never been off Maspin at all. He can fly, though, and when asked where he learned he says a book or two, which is either a joke or the most alarming sentence in the temple.

    Dan TESTIMONY

    full name: Diontesheempluntornskalla

    A councillor of Riflo, and the one who will actually talk to you.

    The full name is real and he does not expect anyone offworld to attempt it. Dan is what he offers, immediately, with no ceremony about it, which is exactly how Maspin names work: the long one is inherited, and the short one is the one that stuck.

    His seat is harmony

    Not defence, not trade, not rites. His job on that Council is the agreement between people, and he holds it because he believes real strength is empathy and restraint rather than the other thing.

    He is the one who collects the Gift of Memory at the festival, and he takes his time about it.

    "Wine allows humans to feel very deeply."

    The decontamination doctor TESTIMONY

    Whoever is on shift at the far end of the Maspin decon cycle, waiting for you to be finished being sick.

    The cycle is thorough. Most first-timers come out of it on their knees, and this one has watched enough of that to have a routine: he waits, he lets you get there yourself, and then he offers a hand and a smirk he does not fully suppress.

    "First time, I take it? Won't take long to get used to. Mind over matter, unless you've got a severe parasite, scales, or plasma burns."

    The Friend TESTIMONY

    the Maspin shaman

    Ask for the shaman on Maspin and you will be corrected. He would rather you called him Friend.

    He smiles in a way people describe, without prompting and in almost the same words, as soft and ancient.

    What he does

    Nobody outside is clear. He is present at the festival, he is consulted about people who are dying, and the Trailblazer surgeon at Base Delta credits him with stopping a man from bleeding out through a hole in the heart, and then walking that man back to a vehicle afterwards.

    Finding him

    You do not. Ask a Maspin child where the shaman is and you will get a straight answer:

    "You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

    Two things that unsettle visitors

    He knows names he has not been told. And he has been known to leave something at the medbay for a person before that person arrived on the world, with instructions about who to say it came from.

    Long service, clean record, and a retirement date.

    At the bar he takes the seat next to whoever is on their own and offers, unprompted, to wingman for them. He plays Mead cards in partners and is a serious loss as a partner, because he narrates his own hand.

    The Ivory Guards INTACT

    The ceremonial line on Shayron, and the most photographed soldiers in the galaxy.

    Pristine ivory armour. Long ceremonial coats that fall past the knee. Helmets built tall enough to add most of a head, kept immaculate, and never once seen with a scuff on them.

    They stand exactly fifty metres apart. Not roughly. Every gap on the approach is the same gap, and the sameness is doing the work: a line of men that regular reads as a fact about the place rather than a decision anyone made.

    Whether they can fight is a question nobody asks, which is the point.

    The pilot. Officially one of twelve attached to the platoon. In practice, when Castle Team goes anywhere, Jax flies them.

    Jimzon Cavaris INTACT

    also: Jim · Jimzy · Jimz · Jimzo · Jimbo · Jimmy

    Twenty-six. Spec Ops Staff Sergeant, and the man the rest of Castle Team follows without anyone ever having decided that.

    Short brown hair. Stubble he never quite gets on top of. He thinks he looks like nobody in particular, and he is wrong about how much that is true.

    Two marks he cannot walk past a mirror without finding. His nose was broken in a fistfight that got away from everybody and set crooked, because nobody thought to have it fixed. There is a thin burn line across his left cheek where the hair does not grow, from too much to drink, a handful of fireworks and the certainty of being twenty and finished with the Academy. Nobody else notices either one.

    His armour is black and deliberately unshined, with a blue visor. He paints it himself, by hand, every time.

    He wears glasses some of the time, and there is no pattern to when.

    Everyone who likes him has a different name for him, and none of them agreed on one. Calsco Fritt calls him something else entirely, on purpose, and waits every single time for the correction that never comes.

    A promotion to Captain is sitting on somebody's desk. He failed officer school once already, years ago, and has not mentioned that in a while.

    Where he is from, and where he is from

    Born on Modanick and has never once set foot on it. What he knows about his own birthworld is a bedtime story his mother told him: always warm, always daytime, trees taller than houses. She was describing a place she had loved as a student to a boy sitting on a rock, and she made it better than it is.

    He grew up on the Corefuel colony in the wreckage of Wake, where his father ran the station. The family was two months from moving to Creta.

    What he carries

    A grey stone he picked up on the colony road when he was eight. He has had it for twenty years and it is smooth because he rubs it. His mother's service pistol, cleaned since he was old enough to be shown how. A gold holowatch, a gift from a general, shined and with an audible tick to it. An engagement ring in a velvet box that has not been opened in front of anybody.

    What he is like

    Impulsive to the point of recklessness, and funnier in private than anyone outside the team would believe. Table impressions. A napkin moustache. A microwave that went out of a window. He reads his own silence as steadiness and does not notice that everyone around him reads it as absence.

    He is casually bigoted about non-humans in the ordinary, unexamined way of somebody raised where he was raised, and he is unthinkingly kind to children, and he would be embarrassed to have either one pointed out.

    He also uses Crag the way everyone he grew up with uses it, and thinks nothing about it at all.

    Karagash RECOVERED

    A Gashi bounty hunter, and the most reasonably priced frightening thing in the sector.

    Seven feet. Strong through the shoulders and the arms without any of the bulk that usually comes attached, so the size does not register properly until he is standing next to something you know the height of. His hand closes on a wrist like a vise closing, and he is fast in a way that people who have watched it are not able to describe afterwards without their voice changing.

    The face

    He wears a mask across the lower half of it, a breathing apparatus rather than a disguise, and it has been there long enough that the shape of him without it is not a thing many people have seen. Above it, gold and black eyes with no pupil anybody has ever managed to find. You can tell exactly when he looks at something, because the light comes off them differently when they move.

    The rest

    Black suits, cut for a human frame and made to fit his, and he wears them well. A bandolier across the chest, which is not strictly necessary and is clearly a thing he enjoys. And ginger hair, deep and well combed and frankly gorgeous, which on a Gashi is normal and on a seven-foot masked man in a black suit is the detail people bring up first.

    The work

    He hunts for hire. He is extremely good at it and he does not extend mercy, and he is also not angry, ever, about any part of it. The two usually travel together and in him they simply do not. He takes the job, states the price, does the job, collects, and wishes you a good one.

    Nobody knows why he went into this line rather than one of the ten thousand respectable ones a Gashi is expected to want. There is speculation and none of it is worth repeating. The likeliest answer is the one that never gets proposed, which is that he tried it and liked it.

    He is, for what it is worth, modestly priced.

    A bounty hunter, and a voice giving orders in a room the record does not describe.

Somebody wants a person found, the price is agreed, and no part of the arrangement requires anybody to explain themselves to a government. There are Guard warrants that get worked this way.     Kelsadria Vot Feentor-Jayzin INTACT

    goes by: Kelsa

    A pilot with Nova Squadron, and the most organised person in any room she is in.

    Pale blonde, worn up in a bun nearly always. Very fit, in the unremarkable way of somebody who does the work and does not discuss it. Striking eyes, and they are never idle: there is always something going on behind them, and it usually arrives on her face a second before she decides whether to say it.

    She reads stern for about a minute. She is not. She laughs softly and easily once she has decided you are worth the trouble, and after that she is one of the most expressive people on the flight line.

    The hair comes down almost never. Underneath, behind the ears, it is dyed a soft light purple, and there is no version of a duty day in which anybody sees it.

    Royal blood, thinly. House Feentor, Jayzin line, which is the kind of descent half the galaxy can claim: it comes with a seat, a small maintenance, and no money worth the name. She has never drawn either.

    Sansvor

    She grew up in a beautiful ruin. Gaslamp streets, cathedrals and libraries still standing with the roofs open to the sky, museums nobody catalogues, art nobody looks at, and weather coming in through the gaps. She went to school in something like a bombed-out palace with eight other children in it. The teachers were good. The building was losing.

    Every adult around her had a theory about what the world should become. None of them had a roof.

    So she wanted a roof. She heard a teacher had flown in the war, got her licence, and joined the Guard for a pension and citizenship for her family on a world where things get fixed. Not patriotism. Arithmetic.

    How she works

    She dumps her shots on the floor at the bar and pulls the disgusted face along with everybody else. She sings karaoke under protest and then sings it properly.Disciplined, methodical, always with a plan and a fallback. The exact inverse of the man she was going to marry, which is why it worked when it worked: she kept him from flying off the handle and he got her out of her own head. When it stopped working, his unpredictability left her with nothing to stand on and her need to know what came next started to feel like pressure.

    She said it out loud once, testing how it sounded: Kelsa Cavaris. I like the sound of that. He never gave her the ring. It is still in the box.

    Her enlistment ends within the year.

    King Matthew INTACT

    The reigning King of the Royal systems, and the man giving the address at the Queen's Anniversary for the fourth year running.

    He holds the ordinary powers of the crown, and one that is not ordinary at all. He alone can proclaim an emergency under the High Emergency Council Act, and on that proclamation everything the crown and parliament hold passes to the High Council sitting on Maldo.

    The Act says how the powers go across. It does not say for how long, how they come back, or who reviews it. This has been raised in parliament four times and amended none.

    It has never been invoked.

    Korjin Cavaris INTACT

    Chemist, engineer, and the man who worked out how to turn the core of a dead planet into fuel.

    He invented the Corefuel synthesis process. Everything that flies, anywhere, runs on the back of what he did in a workshop on a rock, and the licence was signed over to the Guard for a consideration of one credit.

    He ran the extraction station in the Wake field himself. He knew everyone on the colony, he called them by name, and he worked the same hours they did.

    What he was like at the end

    Triumphant. He hit quota, called the entire settlement off work, and ordered a festival for two days later. He had a wife he was plainly still delighted by and two sons, one of whom did not live past five.

    His younger boy asked him, that night, for a spaceship. He did not hesitate for even a moment.

    "Even a spaceship. We're gonna get you one."

    His contract paid on completion of the full year's quota and not a tonne before, which is how these contracts are always written.

    The family was two months from moving to Creta.

    Liles Ninzin INTACT

    Somewhere between forty-five and fifty. A general long enough to be respected, and now the one seat on the Guard's Board of Directors that is not a commercial interest.

    He is the man who lifted the floorboard

    He was on the patrol that reached the Wake colony after the raid, and he found a boy under his mother's body when everyone else had written the settlement off.

    He and his then-girlfriend took the child in. They were barely out of college and doing what they could for someone with nowhere else to go. There was an eighth birthday with a small cake, a cheap dinner, and laughter that felt borrowed and was meant kindly.

    They were always kind, and the kindness is what made the distance worse.

    Now

    He runs interference for Jimzon constantly and cannot say why in those words. He offers him a captaincy, quarters, a ship of his own. He refuses to authorise the hunt for the Nhaths, and then authorises it anyway, off the books, with leave time and no paper trail: I don't need proof that I gave this the OK.

    He notices things. The bottom row of a man's medals in the wrong order, at a glance, across a room.

    He is old enough now that his knees are a running joke between the two of them, and old enough to get nostalgic about the Battle of Rudcuff without noticing he is doing it, in the specific way of a man remembering the last time his job was simple.

    What he says he wants, delivered like warmth:

    "One day I'd like us both to be on the Director Board, together, away from the mess of combat."

    He is on a board of seven where every member can be removed by the other six, and where nobody's dissent has ever been written down.

    The little girl in the waiting room TESTIMONY

    A child in the medbay at Base Delta, with a puzzle in her lap, waiting for her father.

    She looks up at whoever comes in, blinks, tilts her head, and crosses the room with the kind of confidence only children and fools have. Then she sits down opposite you, uninvited, and starts.

    "Are you a clown?"

    She is a hard audience. Told a joke, she does not laugh. Shown a costume flower that honks twice, she does not laugh at that either. Her mouth holds a perfect little frown.

    Then she explains why she is there.

    "My teacher told me my daddy lost his leg. He isn't here yet. My teacher said he walked on a mine." "Mommy was too."

    Her father is a Trailblazer who stepped on a mine. Her mother was one.

    "Daddy really likes his legs. I think he's probably sad now."

    She will laugh, eventually, at a bad enough joke. How much do rainbows weigh? Not much, they are actually pretty light.

    "I will, mister. You're a funny clown."

    We do not have her name. We are not looking for it.

    Maspin children TESTIMONY

    Glowing eyes at knee height, and a giggle that visitors describe as wind moving through a hollow tree.

    They bounce when somebody interesting walks past. They are not shy. And they will tell you things the adults will not, generally without being asked.

    A Second Sergeant of the Royal Shayron Defence Force, under a name that is not the one he was given.
