    Corefuel

    A quarter of a litre of it will run twenty haulers for a hundred years. It is refined out of the core of a dead planet, and there is one planet you are allowed to take it from.

    Yield

    One standard measure, taken as 0.25 litres, is rated by the licensing authority at a commercial hauler fleet of twenty vehicles for approximately one hundred standard years.

    Reserves

    The Wake fragments are assessed at about five thousand years at current rates. It is not scarce. Nothing about this trade is driven by scarcity.

    The licence

    Extraction, synthesis, transport and resale are licensed by the Guard Board of Directors and by nobody else. Duty is charged at the point it comes out of the ground and again at the point it is sold.

    For GC 4461: 812,443.6 tonnes extracted, 40,622,180 credits in duty, and 3,249,774,400 credits at final market.

    Everywhere else

    Every world has a core. Getting at one anywhere else means deep drilling, fracturing, or a lucky asteroid, and then it still has to be synthesised. Since GC 4420 there have been eleven applications for a non-Wake licence. All eleven were withdrawn by the applicant.

    The process

    1 gap

    Registered GC 4417 to a single named patentee, K. Cavaris, and assigned afterwards to the Board for a consideration of one credit. The registration sets the process out in seven steps. Six of them are redacted in the copy we hold. [RECORD DAMAGED]

    What the Maspin say

    That planetary cores are alive. That the thing in the tanks is not a mineral. They do not say it as belief, and mystics on four other worlds say something close enough that we have filed them together, under religious testimony, which is where claims go when nothing corroborates them.

    [Compiler's note: the market figure above is filed to the credit. The number of people employed in the extraction zone is not filed at all.]

    The Council Chamber of Riflo

    Stone floor, woven banners, and bioluminescent vines kept trained along the upper walls, so the whole room has a faint blue underlight before anyone lights anything.

    A ceremonial bowl sits in the centre. When it is lit at the opening of a session, every seated councillor's flame answers it, each one a different colour, and the room reads at a glance as a set of individuals rather than a body.

    The floor hums

    Everyone who has stood in that chamber says so, and none of them says it as a figure of speech. The stone carries the mood of the room. Anger, amusement, doubt, all of it comes up through your feet before anybody speaks.

    Records are taken by hand with feathered quills. Gavels are used. A vote is not counted; the flames change colour, and unanimity is all of them going white at once.

    The Council of Riflo

    Governing council of the settled belt, Maspin. Composition is by seat rather than by election, and the Restoration has not established how a seat is filled.

    Address

    Councillors are addressed as the Council and by nothing else. They do not give their names to outsiders and they do not appear to use them with each other in session. This is a rule of the body, not a courtesy, and no visitor has ever been given the reason for it.

    Seats

    Nobody outside Maspin knows how many there are or how you get one. Seats are not elected in any sense a visitor would recognise, are not obviously inherited, and are not explained. What is known is that one of them belongs to the Trailblazers, has since GC 4451, and is held by a human, which suggests the body can add a seat when it decides to.

    This is a remote world that has had very few long-term visitors and no interest in being surveyed. Almost everything in this entry comes from people who were guests.

    Proceedings

    Catalogued under the Council Chamber. Decision is expressed through the councillors' flames. Unanimity is described as their merging to a single white.

    Competences, as reported

    Taxation and remittance to the Royal treasury. Land and concession. Labour, including the administration of indenture. Rites and observance. Relief.

    Relief

    The Council's own submissions to the Royal treasury are held here in copy and record fourteen applications for assistance over nineteen years following eruption, quake, flood and crop loss. No reply to any of them is held by this archive, and the Council states that none was received.

    Indenture

    Administered by the Council. The Restoration notes, from the Council's own registers, that indentured persons are in a number of recorded cases assigned to establishments controlled by the family of a sitting councillor. The registers record this openly, there being no provision under which it would need to be concealed.

    Crag

    The slur. It means non-human, all of them, any of them.

    It is not a word for a species. It is a word for a category, and it gets used identically on peoples who have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. A Nhath and a Vitula and a Targath share no biology, no history and no language, and one syllable covers all three.

    Where it came from

    Nobody knows. There is no first use, no derivation, and nobody who can tell you. It shows up in the recovered material already in general circulation, with no gloss, as though it never needed one.

    The exemption

    People who use it will very often exempt somebody. This one is different. This one is all right. It is offered as a compliment and taken as one, and it does not reduce how often the word gets used. It is what lets everyone go on using it.

    Where it sits

    It is not in Galactic Standard law. Nothing prohibits it. Guard notices discourage it in the messes, which are the only official documents anywhere that admit the word exists, and they are notices about language rather than about people.

    Non-humans are about a fifth of everyone alive. They are 0.8 per cent of the Guard.

    Creta

    Green mountains, lakes you can see the bottom of, and spring that does not end. Four continents, four governments, and more money than any of them will discuss.

    Four countries, one policy

    The continents govern themselves and have agreed on foreign policy by permanent convention, renewed without amendment forty-one times. What they argue about instead, in the record and in public, is fishing quota, water rights, and the correct preparation of two dishes.

    Neutral, and armed about it

    Creta was not invaded, not blockaded and not bombarded, through the entire war. Its own account credits universal service sized to make occupation expensive, and a standing refusal of basing rights to anybody.

    Both belligerents also banked here throughout. We record that as a second fact and not as a correction to the first.

    Service is eleven months and universal. The force has no long-range transport, no expeditionary doctrine, and no legal power to acquire either.

    The vaults

    Cretan deposit records survived the Wipe because they were on paper in rooms built to survive things. The four governments state that they are complete. They are not open to this archive, to the Guard, or to anyone else. Applications are answered promptly and in the negative.

    The giving

    Endowment records are public and precise. Between GC 4403 and 4462 Cretan foundations paid for 1,206 libraries, 411 hospitals and 89 university faculties on other worlds. Where the underlying capital came from is not published.

    [Compiler's note: this society works from three rooms. Two of them were paid for by a Cretan endowment. We record that here because it seemed dishonest not to.]

    Custodial labour

    Prison work. Not a camp exactly, and not a prison exactly either.

    A sentence can be extended by administrative decision on grounds set out in a schedule. The grounds are broad, the decision is not appealable, and the numbers are unambiguous: 41,206 terms extended over twenty years, against 88 reduced.

    Where

    Two Guard installations take most of it. One of them mines magnetic ore. What that ore is for does not appear anywhere.

    Who

    The rolls are kept by species. Non-humans are about a fifth of everyone alive and about three fifths of these rolls. Targath turn up at a rate the population numbers cannot account for.

    Why it is defended

    Guard material puts it in terms of the bigger picture: the work needs doing, the sentences exist anyway, and member states that fall behind on their obligations can be reminded that both of those things are true.

    Daiser

    Caretaker of the Council's temple at Riflo, and the sharpest person in the building.

    He is introduced to offworlders as the Gatekeeper, which is what the job is called and not what he is. He opens the great oak doors, receives you, and shows you where to stand, and it is very easy to treat him as furniture for the first ten minutes.

    "He's not just a gatekeeper. His name is Daiser. He's... like you. Someone surviving the pressure. Don't add more weight to his shoulders."

    A Maspin: smoke and vapour, water where the eyes should be, an ember behind it all that brightens when he is enjoying himself, which is often.

    The situation

    He is indentured. Sentenced to work off a debt that exists on paper and nowhere else, with seven years still on it and no wage to buy it out with. His holder is an establishment controlled by his own uncle, who sits on the Council. Everybody involved regards this as normal, including, most of the time, Daiser.

    "We call it indentured servitude. Where I work off an imaginary debt until I can pay it off and be free, which is actually fucking hard without a paycheck."

    Before that

    A chemist, and a properly trained one. He can make things most people cannot get, including weapons that are banned on his own world.

    How he talks

    Two registers, switched instantly. Street with anyone he likes. An elaborate, over-polished formal voice for anyone with authority, deployed with a completely straight face, which is its own kind of insult.

    He has never flown. He has never been off Maspin at all.He has never been off Maspin at all. He can fly, though, and when asked where he learned he says a book or two, which is either a joke or the most alarming sentence in the temple.

    The Dead Moon raiders

    White cloaks in a whiteout, black masks with nothing on them but metal eyepieces, long rifles with bayonets fixed.

    Not a species. A faction, drawn from several populations of the cold outer moons, and beyond that nobody knows how it is put together. No structure, no leader, no territory, no demand has ever been recorded. They do not hold ground and do not appear to want any.

    Everybody who has survived contact says the same thing about the way they move, which is that they are in no hurry. They come out of the storm at a walk.

    The one thing that stops them

    Missionaries reached those moons out of Sonaff, and a number of raider populations hold the same faith as communities they are otherwise permanently at war with. There is at least one recorded case of a raider breaking off in the middle of an action on seeing a devotional pendant.

    Not surrender, not mercy, not law. A pendant.

    The decontamination doctor

    The Destruction of Wake

    The most talked-about event in living memory, and the one nobody can agree on.

    What the Guard says

    One ordnance deployment, Autumnal forces, GC 4394. Over in under an hour. Responsibility stated flatly, with no source cited and no unit named. It appears as settled fact in every piece of Guard educational material.

    What the people say

    We collected thirty-eight accounts across eleven settlements and six worlds, all of them from people who were children then or repeating a parent. Every single one describes something that took days. Two to nine of them. Six say the sky changed colour before anything was heard. Four describe evacuation orders. One describes those orders being cancelled.

    An hour and nine days are not two versions of one event.

    We note, and draw nothing from it, that the account was published by the party that later received the exclusive licence to mine the remains, and that there is nobody left on the other side to answer it.

    How many died

    Between 900 million and 4 billion. Neither number rests on a document. Both rest on people.

    Dragon's blood trees

    Broad flat canopies on bare trunks, named for the red resin that runs when you cut them. Slow, long-lived, and entirely happy in ruined ground.

    Which is why Sansvor is full of them now. They have come up inside two rail terminals, an exchange and eleven civic buildings, and in every case the municipality entered them as a maintenance item and then left them alone. The canopy of the north terminal is a tree.

    The resin sells as a varnish and a dye. It is the world's largest surviving export by value, which says more about the world than about the resin.

    Dreamwalking

    The belief that the soul is tied to the body rather than kept inside it, and that in deep sleep or unconsciousness the tie goes slack.

    While it is slack the soul can be moved. Including, adherents say, through time.

    The mechanics they describe

    Consciousness has something like weight, and that weight pulls it back toward its body. Overcome the pull and it goes elsewhere. A stretch of unconsciousness earlier in your life leaves the body unoccupied for that long, and that unoccupied time stays available afterwards. Two days in a coma at twenty buys you two days at forty, and while you are using them you are twenty.

    They also hold that this was once done with instruments rather than by accident, and that a device existed for pointing a soul somewhere rather than merely loosening it.

    Where it turns up

    Among Maspin practitioners working with floom preparations, in two monastic traditions on Shayron, and in the folk medicine of four worlds with no connection to each other.

    Why we have not dismissed it

    Religious testimony is normally consistent about meaning and wildly inconsistent about mechanism. This is the other way round. The accounts agree in detail about how it is supposed to work and disagree about what it is for, and we do not know what to make of that.

    The Elder Tree

    One tree, hollow at the base, going up into cloud. Inside it there is a chamber with mosaic walls and a chandelier, and in the middle of the floor there is a hole.

    Inside

    Every account agrees on the room: the mosaic, the light hanging above, humans and Maspin standing together with no arrangement made for either, and the opening at the centre with nothing around it.

    Height

    Nobody has measured it. Every informant describes the crown entering cloud. Trailblazer survey work in the surrounding concession recorded canopy heights across the district and stopped at the edge of the ceremonial ground, by agreement.

    What it is for

    The dead go into the hole. Blue vapour comes back up afterwards and is taken into the tree. The Maspin hold that what goes down returns to the ocean beneath the crust and that the tree drinks from it.

    One thing we can add

    The district around this tree is exceptionally fertile, and nothing is imported into it.

    Attributed to C., Base Delta, and to four Maspin informants who asked to be recorded together.

    The Elder Tree interment rite

    How the Maspin bury their dead, which is not burial.

    The chamber fills. Somebody starts singing and the room takes it up. The person being interred walks to the edge of the opening in the floor and sings over it. Then the hood comes down, the necklace comes off and is set on the ground, and they step backward into the hole.

    Blue steam comes up afterwards and the tree takes it in.

    The stone from the necklace goes into the wall.

    Everyone attends

    Humans, Maspin, anybody who is there. Nothing is arranged differently for outsiders and nobody is warned in advance what they are about to watch. Two of the three visitors who described this to us had no idea what was happening until it had happened.

    They walk

    Every account has the person going to the edge unassisted and stepping back on their own. We asked, as plainly as we could manage, whether the timing is chosen by the person being interred. They understood the question perfectly well. They did not think it was an important one.

    Even graves grow flowers, I may sink like a stone, For what we know, for what we know, But you'll never be alone.

    The enlistment rites form

    Six questions you answer on your first day, about your own body.

    Burned or buried. Which faith, from a list of eighty-eight, with a blank line if yours is not on it. Whether your family wants you sent home at their own cost. Two names. Your signature. The date.

    You cannot start without filling it in, and once filed it is kept forever, because decades later it is the document somebody reads to find out what to do with you.

    It can be changed at any time by writing in. Fewer than two people in a hundred ever do.

    [Compiler's note: it is a good form. It is well drafted and it is honoured. The volunteer transcribing the GC 4444 series stopped for the day when she noticed what the ages in the third column were.]

    Cross-reference

      Fermented kraskor

      The finest thing on Maspin, by the Council's own account, and it is meat that has been left alone for years.

      Kraskor flesh is fermented down until it is liquid, or near enough, and then taken the way Maspin take everything, which is absorbed rather than eaten. Grades exist and the good ones are measured in years.

      The Council's formal submissions describe it, alongside pickled inside-barked mycelium, as a staple delicacy of the cuisine. That is the highest praise any food gets in a Maspin document.

      None of it is exported. What leaves this world is live kraskor, in a form the Maspin themselves would not touch.

      Floom eggs

      Unfertilised eggs, laid on dead ground, full of a blue liquid. On Maspin they are fertiliser. Off Maspin they are the most valuable medicine in existence.

      The ordinary use is the important one: a floom drops them on dry grass or a failing garden and a week later the ground has recovered. That is how the settled belt stays fertile without importing anything.

      The fluid

      Nobody sensible calls it a drug. Calsco calls it the essence of life in its purest form and does not appear to be exaggerating for effect. It is the medium in the sensory tanks and it brings people back from injuries that should have finished them.

      Taking it

      For a human it is hours of something that is not a high in any recognisable sense. For a Maspin it is not hours. Ask one whether they have ever tried it and you will get a straight no, and the reason, which is that the effect would last the rest of their life.

      Control

      The Council of Riflo restricts collection, holding and export, and has refused three applications to expand the trade. It is the most valuable thing on the planet, and the body sitting on it is the body that would profit most from letting it go.

      Flooms

      The creature Maspin runs on, and the reason the air there is as good as it is.

      They are nervous, affectionate, and much smarter than they look. Everyone who has kept them says the same thing, unprompted: a floom decides very quickly what it thinks of a person, and it is almost never wrong. People on Maspin take this seriously enough to act on it.

      What they do

      They take in ambient life energy the way a plant takes light. Not stealing it, not draining anything, just standing in it.

      Then they lay eggs on dead ground: unfertilised, full of a blue liquid, dropped on dry grass and failing gardens. About a week later the ground has come back greener than it was. The Trailblazer concession imports no fertiliser at all and its yields keep climbing.

      The local phrasing, given to us word for word by three different people:

      Floom is the ecosystem. All things live because of flooms, and floom lives because of life.

      Trade

      They are exported, in very small numbers. The Council restricts it and has turned down three applications to expand it.

      Foundation Day

      The Guard's birthday, and the best-documented event in this volume by an enormous margin.

      Same date every year since GC 4406. Assembly at nine, an address by whichever Director is nearest, a parade, a flyover if there is a fleet in the system, food for everybody, and a broadcast in the evening. It is not a religious holiday and the Guard is clear about that.

      It is also observed almost everywhere. Twelve member worlds hold it on a different local date, for harvest or weather reasons, each by a written dispensation, each of which we have.

      Why we hold so much of it

      Because the Guard photographed itself. We have the incorporation papers, the register of all fifty-six observances, the parade orders, the vendor licences, the road closures, the catering invoices, and 4,192 photographic plates.

      Attendance at the main event last year: 218,406, counted at the gate.

      [Compiler's note: this entry took an afternoon. The one after it in this volume took nine years and is four sentences long.]

      The Friend

      the Maspin shaman

      Ask for the shaman on Maspin and you will be corrected. He would rather you called him Friend.

      He smiles in a way people describe, without prompting and in almost the same words, as soft and ancient.

      What he does

      Nobody outside is clear. He is present at the festival, he is consulted about people who are dying, and the Trailblazer surgeon at Base Delta credits him with stopping a man from bleeding out through a hole in the heart, and then walking that man back to a vehicle afterwards.

      Finding him

      You do not. Ask a Maspin child where the shaman is and you will get a straight answer:

      "You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

      Two things that unsettle visitors

      He knows names he has not been told. And he has been known to leave something at the medbay for a person before that person arrived on the world, with instructions about who to say it came from.

      Galactic Standard

      What everybody speaks. Nobody made them.

      No law imposes it and no instrument requires it. It is the language of the code, the ledger, the shipping manifests and the Guard, and that has been more than enough. If you want to buy something, sue somebody, or get paid, this is the language you do it in.

      It is getting more uniform every year

      The teaching material for the member worlds is produced centrally, and comparing recovered pre-war regional speech against what people say now shows a large number of local features gone inside two generations.

      What that costs

      Our survey lists sixty-one languages and dialects that were alive in somebody's memory and had no living speaker by the time we got there. The rate is highest on worlds where the schools were handed to sponsored foundations on contract, and the correlation is strong enough to mention while being careful not to call it a cause.

      In court

      Proceedings are in Galactic Standard, and translation is at your own expense unless you are the accused in a criminal matter, in which case it is provided.

      Galactic Standard law

      The code that runs everywhere, sitting on top of whatever your own world does.

      A member world writes its own statutes and the Guard leaves them alone. It can strike any of them at any time and in fifty-three years has done so forty-one times, thirty-eight of which were about tax or port dues, because that is what the Guard actually minds about.

      The part that matters

      The code applies everywhere. Enforcement does not, and nothing in the code requires it to. There is no provision for complaining that a law was applied to you and not your neighbour, and no body that would hear it.

      So automatic plasma weapons are lawful under local statute on nineteen worlds and unlawful under the code on all of them, and both facts sit there until somebody needs one of them. A world can run for decades doing something openly and then find out it was illegal the whole time, on the day that becomes useful.

      The laws are not there to be applied. They are there to be available.

      Slavery

      Prohibited absolutely, in the strongest language in the entire code. There is no inspectorate, no penalty schedule, and no enforcement mechanism attached to it.

      The Gashi

      Green-skinned, and nobody can agree on whether that skin is reptile or amphibian.

      Up close it settles the question no better. It has the fine dry grain of scale in some lights and the give of something that would rather be damp in others, and the Gashi themselves find the question tedious in the way any people find it tedious when strangers open with it.

      What they wear

      Robes and tunics, cut long, and over them a great deal of decorative gear that is built to move: panels, sashes, hanging lengths of fabric weighted at the ends so they swing and settle rather than hang dead. A Gashi walking across a room is doing something that a human walking across a room is not.

      The hair

      All colours, every variety, and no two families the same. What is consistent is the quality of it. Gashi hair grows thick, holds a shape, takes a comb, and looks in every case as though it has just been finished by somebody very good, which is not a thing they work at and is very annoying to everyone else.

      What they do

      Artisans, overwhelmingly, in the broad sense rather than the narrow one. Chefs, painters, teachers, engravers, people who make the small good version of a thing that could have been made badly and cheaply instead. It is a whole world, so it is also farmers and clerks and mechanics, but the culture is built around art and sophistication and it judges accordingly.

      Which makes the ones who go into other lines of work interesting, because the sophistication does not come off. It just gets applied to something else.

      The gem mosaic wall

      The inside of the Elder Tree is covered in coloured stones, and every one of them is a person.

      When a Maspin is interred, the stone is taken off the necklace they wore in life and set into the wall. There are thousands. Nobody has counted them and nobody has been asked to.

      There is no order to it. Not by date, not by family, not by anything. A stone goes wherever there is room. There are no names, no dates, and no inscriptions of any kind, so a family cannot come back and find their own.

      Asked about that, they say it is not what the wall is for.

      The gem-setting practice

      Every Maspin wears a stone. When they die, it goes into the wall.

      It is taken off the necklace they wore in life and set by somebody from the household, or by a councillor, wherever there happens to be room. No inscription, no date, nothing written at all.

      Asked how a family finds their own stone afterwards, they said that they do not, and looked mildly puzzled that anyone would want to.

      The Gift of Memory

      You do not tell a Maspin what happened to you. You give them a tear and they feel it.

      Do not tell. Share a tear.

      At the festival someone comes to collect it. You hold a memory, a real one, whatever moves you, and it goes into a single tear, and that is taken. Love, grief, joy, the worst thing you have ever seen. The kind does not matter.

      It has to be true

      A memory picked for effect is detectable, is an insult, and the Maspin will not explain how they know.

      What it is for

      It is how they come to understand another person. They do not assume understanding and they do not ask for it. It is given once, deliberately, and it costs the giver something to hand over.

      The Council asks for one from foreign parties. It sits in the minutes alongside credits and shipping like any other term of an agreement, because to the Maspin it is one.

      Several cultures in this volume forbid a person from ever speaking about certain things. When someone from one of those worlds gives this gift, they have not found a clever way around their own rule. They have broken it.

      Glazberries

      Small teal berries with a hard glossy skin, bitter enough raw to make you pull a face, and good cooked or fermented.

      They grow wild on several jungle worlds and are farmed properly on Kinton. Their real distinction is that almost everybody can eat them: they agree with humans and with most surveyed physiologies, which is rare enough that three separate services put them in the standard field ration.

      The Grand Mothership Dining Hall

      Warm tans and golds, in a ship that is otherwise white and blue all the way through. It is the only room aboard that does not look like a machine.

      It seats the entire embarked complement in three sittings, and it cost more to fit out than the medical wing, which is in the accounts and has never been commented on.

      You are required to come out of armour to eat. The standing order gives the reason as morale, and it is correct: it is the one hour of the day when a unit stops looking like a unit and starts looking like five people who know each other.

      Graves

      The oldest of the five sent to Sonaff, which is why he ended up in charge of them.

      Nobody appointed him. There were five people in a blizzard outside a sealed hangar, not one of them infantry, and he was the one who had been in longest, so he gave the orders.

      That is the entire plan, and given what he had to work with it is not a bad one.

      Gravity spires

      Towers that burn Corefuel to hold an atmosphere onto a rock that has no business keeping one.

      A spire generates a local gravitational field and a pressure envelope around itself, about 1.4 kilometres across. Put three to seven of them in a cluster with overlapping envelopes and you can live on an asteroid: walk outside, plant a garden, hang washing.

      They are how the Wake fragment colonies existed at all. The homeworld's own core, refined, keeping the people standing on its wreckage alive.

      What breaks

      The regulator assembly, always. Nobody can make one; they come out of salvage and pre-war stock, issued quarterly against a settlement's entitlement.

      What happens if a cluster goes

      The envelope opens over four to eleven hours depending on its size. The safety schedule says get to a hardened structure. It does not say what to do after that.

      The Great War

      also known as: the War · the Last War · the Long Account (Katanzaria)

      Two powers went to war and both of them ceased to exist. Nothing succeeded either one. Everything in this volume is dated from it and nobody can tell you why it started.

      When

      It stopped in GC 4402 and no source disputes that. It started somewhere between GC 4386 and GC 4393 depending on which world you ask, a spread of seven years. Some of that is worlds dating the war from the first fighting in their own sky. Not all of it is.

      Why

      Every world has an answer. No two answers agree. No document has been recovered that would let anyone prefer one.

      Our view, marked as inference and held loosely: this is not lost data. There was never one story to lose. INFERRED

      How it was fought

      Look at the requisitions and the damage assessments and the targets come up in the same order every time: shipyards, weapons manufacture, plasma extraction, medicine, banks. Ground taken and ground lost barely appear.

      They were not trying to hold each other's worlds. They were taking each other's capacity to make things, and they succeeded, and that is why a galaxy that can still fly cannot build a ship.

      Who was on which side

      We cannot draw the map. The best evidence is tax filings, because allegiance was decided by whom you paid, and they give roughly 65 worlds one way and 72 the other with everything else neutral, split, or paying both.

      Nineteen worlds appear in the collection records of both parties in the same year.

      The two atrocities

      The Wipe, laid at C.O.R.D.'s door. The destruction of Wake, laid at the Autumnals'. In both cases the accusation is made by the other side, and in one of those cases the other side is not there to answer it.

      [Compiler's note: we have been asked several times to produce a map. We have not produced a map.]

      Greyleaf

      Cured leaf, rolled and smoked. The most common vice in the galaxy and the cheapest.

      Grown on forty-one worlds, sold everywhere by the packet, legal in every jurisdiction in this volume, and issued as part of the Guard ration. It is what two people share on a wall at the end of a shift.

      It also turns up in the cause-of-death column on every member world that keeps one.

      Reader's key

      Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 30.

      The Guard

      A police force on a small world with a port, which is now the largest thing in the galaxy. It did not fight the war. It was incorporated four years after the war stopped, by people who had.

      Founding

      The incorporation instrument survives and names nine founders by name and prior title. Four were general officers of armies that no longer existed. Five held commercial interests in shipping, insurance and salvage.

      It constitutes the body as a chartered corporation selling security to subscribing worlds. That is what it is. Everything since has been growth.

      The first world is not named in the instrument, and we have not been able to establish it.

      What you get for joining

      Defence, and free movement of persons between every member world.

      Read the accession debates and it is the second one they talk about. We hold eleven in full, and in nine of them the right to go somewhere is the argument that carries the vote. That is what a galaxy remembers after it has watched borders decide who lived.

      What you give

      An assessed share of revenue, and people. Your own laws, religion, holidays and government stay yours. Planetary law can be struck by the Guard at any time and almost never is, because the Guard wants the money and not the argument.

      Not an army, a company

      There are no branches. Flight, ground, engineering, medical and administrative divisions share the same hull, the same mess and the same seniority list. Nobody serves in a national contingent; absorbed formations enter as individuals, which is why no formation in the establishment is older than the Guard itself.

      Not enlistment, contract

      Fixed term, completion bonus per operation. Units bid for the work that is going, and units with strong completion records win what they bid on. Acceptance rates are filed by unit.

      Nobody is assigned. Everybody applies.

      Standing order 41

      Materiel at a cleared objective is recovered rather than destroyed, and a schedule sets out what the recovering personnel may keep. The schedule has been widened twice. Retained items are not entered anywhere, on the stated ground that entering them would be disproportionate.

      Enforcement

      Galactic Standard law is universal and binding. Nothing in it requires enforcement to be even, provides a complaint for uneven enforcement, or names a body to hear one.

      The laws are not there to be applied. They are there to be available.

      The Guard Academy

      Where the Guard raises the people it will employ.

      Two ways in. The ordinary one is an application at the usual age from a member world. The other is wardship: when an action leaves a child with nobody, and the Guard was there, the Guard takes the child.

      Over the last twenty years that is 41,880 children. The average age when they come in is seven.

      They get a real education, better than most worlds manage, plus service instruction from about twelve and a specialist stream from fifteen. Poetry, mathematics, languages, the lot. Eleven periods across the entire course are spent on the history of the Great War.

      Ordinary entrants join the service at a rate of about six in ten. Wardship entrants join at ninety-four in a hundred, which is not surprising, because the Academy is the only home they have.

      The Guard Board of Directors

      Seven people run the galaxy. They elected each other, and any of them can be removed by the other six.

      That is the whole constitution and it has never been amended. No member world confirms them. No citizen votes on them. There is no term, no appeal, and nobody outside the room to appeal to.

      What they hold

      The money. Every exclusive licence the Guard owns, including Corefuel. Every senior appointment. Authorisation of any operation above a certain size. Standing orders. And the power to strike any law on any member world.

      Who they are

      People with commercial interests, undeclared, because nothing requires them to declare and nothing requires Guard contracts to be advertised. One seat has always gone to a general, which the founding document does not require and which has happened every time anyway.

      What the minutes look like

      In nineteen years, 1,411 resolutions. 1,388 of them carried without a division, which means nobody asked for a count. There is no way to record a dissent on the form and nobody has ever asked for one to be added.

      Seven people who can each be fired by the other six will agree with each other about almost everything. Not because they are told to. Because none of them wants to be the one who objected.

      Guard burial rites

      Whatever you wrote on the form when you signed, the Guard does. That is the promise and it is kept.

      Cremation or burial, your faith or none of them, a plot on the Burial Moon at no cost, your remains transported, and two family members brought out at the Guard's expense to stand there.

      Anything beyond that is chargeable: a custom stone, a particular plot, a third relative, or sending you home to your own world instead.

      When there are no remains

      The obligation is discharged with a service and no interment, and the name goes onto the memorial walls at the annual addition like everyone else.

      When there are too many

      One paragraph in the schedule permits a single combined service, at the caretakers' discretion, when the numbers are past what the moon can handle.

      It has been used.

      Guard credits

      The money. There is no coin, no note, and nothing you can hold. A credit is a line in the Guard's ledger and it is worth something because the Guard says it is.

      When the Wipe took every financial record in existence, money went back to paper for about a decade while the accounts were retyped, and then the credit replaced it. It is not backed by metal or grain or anything else. It is backed by the Guard's word and by the fact that member worlds collect tax in it.

      Where it works

      Wherever Guardnet reaches. Beyond that you settle in paper and hope somebody reconciles it later, at the discretion of whoever you are dealing with.

      Which means the answer to whether your savings exist depends on where you are standing. Cut a world off the network and everything its people own becomes a rumour until it comes back.

      The ledger rules allow settlement to a world or a district to be suspended by administrative decision. It has happened nineteen times in twenty years, for an average of forty-one days.

      The Guard franchise

      Everybody votes, the votes are counted honestly, and the count is published. There is no fraud in this entry.

      Every Guard citizen of age gets one vote. Citizenship of your own planet gets you nothing here; you can hold local office on it and still not vote in a Guard poll. Registers are kept by the worlds and audited by the Guard, and fifty-three years of returns exist for every world and district, with the question printed in full.

      What gets voted on

      Over the last twenty years: 88 polls on roads and transit works, 61 on drug licensing, 44 on municipal boundaries, 39 on holidays and observance dates, 31 on harbour works, 22 on schools, and 106 on assorted local statute.

      What does not

      Appropriations. Licensing. Who sits on the Board. Standing orders. Whether an operation happens.

      Turnout averages 79.4 per cent and has been climbing for a decade. People vote because voting works. The things they vote on are the things nobody upstairs minds losing.

      The Guard nurses

      Two of them, on the same ward, and the most frightening thing about them is how ordinary the work is.

      A man comes off a transport screaming and thrashing. They take an arm each and pin him to a thin mattress, and they do it the way two people carry a table through a doorway they have carried tables through before. No hesitation, no signal between them, nothing said.

      Then the respirator, then the sedative, then the next one.

      Guardnet

      The network being built to replace the one that died, and it is not going quickly.

      It carries the credit ledger, service records, licensing and official traffic. It does not carry public communication and was never meant to. If you want to send a letter to someone three systems away you still use a courier ship or a church-owned radio tower, the same as everybody has for sixty years.

      Coverage is continuous through the inner member worlds, patchy past them, and absent on forty-four member worlds and every non-member world in existence.

      That map matters more than anything else about it. Money is a ledger entry now, and the ledger lives here. Where the network reaches, you have savings. Where it does not, you have a promise.

      Hada Mariner

      Long service, clean record, and a retirement date.

      At the bar he takes the seat next to whoever is on their own and offers, unprompted, to wingman for them. He plays Mead cards in partners and is a serious loss as a partner, because he narrates his own hand.

      He is going to Maldo, to one of the ex-Guard communities there, on a square with ornate geometric stonework that he has apparently described to people more than once.

      Maldo is the old Royal capital: a city built out of a used-up world, which stopped making anything a long time ago and is now a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from. A man spends a career on a ship that never stops moving and picks somewhere that has already finished.

      Maspin locals near the Trailblazer base, and the household the medevac dispatcher guesses first.

      Nothing about them is on record except that. When a call comes in from that stretch of country, the voice on the other end says, without checking anything:

      "Is it the Halgo family again?"

      Which tells you the shape of them without a single name. Somebody in that house is always doing something. It has been going on long enough that a bored woman on a radio has stopped needing to look it up.

      The High Castle

      The crown's house on Shayron. Four wings around a court, raised across two centuries in four separate building campaigns, none of which matched the last.

      The bones of it are Maldo steel, shipped in from the old capital while that world still had an industry. The eastern towers are the oldest section standing and carry more of the original metal than anything else in the building.

      That matters more than it sounds. Maldo ore is worked out. There is no more of that steel anywhere, so every repair since has been made in some other alloy that does not quite match, and the maintenance records track the building as a falling percentage of itself.

      The court and the western wing open to the public eleven days a year. The rest is the household's.

      The High Council

      The senior ministers, the service chiefs, and the heads of the great houses, sitting on Maldo. Ordinarily they advise. They do not legislate and they do not command.

      Except

      The High Emergency Council Act says that if the sovereign proclaims an emergency, everything the crown and parliament hold passes to this Council.

      The Act is precise about the proclamation and precise about the transfer. It says nothing about how long it lasts, how it ends, who reviews it, or what would revoke it. Parliament on Maldo has noticed this out loud four times, most recently in GC 4438, and amended it none.

      And the geography

      The Act moves power to a body sitting on Maldo. The sovereign proclaims from Shayron. Those are not in the same system.

      It has never been invoked.

      House Polaris

      The family that took a star's name, and now owns what grows under it.

      They were working that system a thousand years before they were royal. The oldest instruments are commercial and show a family adopting the name of the sun they happened to be under. They have not held land there in a very long time and they hold the licence on everything the system produces.

      Royalty on the Polaris harvest last year: 411,880,600 credits. That is more than the entire assessed revenue of nine member worlds.

      The bit that bothers people

      The star, the system, the shared calendar across ten inhabited bodies, and the family collecting on all of it carry the same word. Nobody in the breadbasket can name the sun that feeds them without naming the house that owns the shelf it sits on.

      Out on the moons the older common word for the sun is still in use in daily speech. It appears in no contract, no ledger and no filing, and three separate people told us the same thing about it: you do not use it in front of buyers.

      Hoverboards

      Everybody knows what one is. Everybody has seen one. Nobody can build one.

      The repulsor assembly came out of factories that no longer exist, and the design is well understood in the sense that engineers can explain exactly how it works and cannot produce the part. Surviving boards get repaired and traded and the price goes up every single year.

      Saigo has tried to rebuild them four times and abandoned it four times. The programme reports are unusually honest about why.

      Humanist supremacy

      That humans are a superior order of thing, that spreading through the stars is theirs by right, and that whatever was done to get here needed no excuse.

      It is not a religion anyone joins

      There is no body, no clergy, no rite, no text, no register. There is nothing to sign.

      It is also the single most widely expressed belief in this volume. It turns up unprompted in testimony from every human world we have surveyed, almost always from people who would tell you flatly that they hold no religious position of any kind.

      How it sounds

      Recorded word for word, on worlds with no contact with one another: that we are a near-perfect design. That the stars were left for us. That whatever happened, it got us here.

      Nobody teaches it and nobody argues with it

      No institution in this archive professes it. No institution in this archive contradicts it. Guard educational material describes human achievement in terms we have difficulty telling apart from the doctrine, and files it under history.

      Humans

      Four out of every five people alive. Present on every inhabited world in this volume except eleven.

      Where from

      Wake, by general account, on the strength of pre-war genetic sampling that we have the conclusions of and not the method. The technique is lost, so the finding cannot be checked, and at least one very populous world rejects it outright. That is why this entry is filed as contested and not because the question is genuinely open.

      Colour does not matter here

      Human populations vary continuously in colouring, height and feature, everywhere, and no world in this archive organises status around it. No statute anywhere in our holdings mentions it. Every planet is mixed and nobody thinks about it.

      What humans sort each other by instead is world, bloodline, profession and service, and those they enforce, sometimes at law. A Modanicker will not let you hold municipal office. Katanzaria will not give you standing without lineage. Marfeld will not call you a man until you have walked into the country alone.

      The word

      Crag, for anyone who is not human, is a human coinage in general human use, and it is universal for exactly the reason the first line of this entry gives. When four fifths of everyone is one thing, that thing stops noticing itself.

      Hyperspace slipstream

      The principal means of interstellar travel. Not motion through space in the ordinary sense.

      Principle

      The vessel does not traverse the distance. The space behind the vessel is drawn toward it. The standard illustration in the navigational primers is that one does not walk to the object; the object is brought.

      Drives

      Classes 1 to 7 are in service. Classes above 4 appear in the underwriters' schedule of unreplaceable classes and no facility for their manufacture is known to survive. Classes 1 to 4 are in production, at three facilities, at a combined annual output the returns record as insufficient to replace annual losses.

      Lanes

      The pre-war lane archive was lost with everything else in GC 4401. The present lanes were re-surveyed by hand over approximately thirty years, at a cost in vessels and crews which the survey authority publishes and which the Restoration has verified against the loss returns.

      Restricted volumes

      The navigational schedules carry standing advisories against transit of certain volumes. Reasons are given for most.

      Indentured servitude

      Working off a debt. Legal everywhere, including on the worlds that advertise themselves as slave-free.

      The distinction that makes it lawful is that you are not owned. You owe. The debt can be one you took on, one somebody assigned to you, one you inherited, or one a court handed you instead of a prison sentence.

      How you get out

      You do not get paid, so the debt comes down by the value of your labour at a rate somebody else sets. We looked at eighty-eight indenture registers. In sixty-one of them the instrument does not state the rate at all.

      Recorded terms run from eleven months to thirty-one years. The middle of that is nine.

      Who runs it

      Whoever the local authority is. On Maspin that is the Council of Riflo, whose own registers show indentured people assigned to households belonging to sitting councillors, written down plainly in the ordinary column, because nothing requires anyone to hide it.

      What the Guard says

      That it is going to be ended, and that the priority is first finishing membership and building a uniform register, after which measures will follow. That position has been published in materially identical words in GC 4429, 4437, 4448 and 4459.

      The Ivory Guards

      The ceremonial line on Shayron, and the most photographed soldiers in the galaxy.

      Pristine ivory armour. Long ceremonial coats that fall past the knee. Helmets built tall enough to add most of a head, kept immaculate, and never once seen with a scuff on them.

      They stand exactly fifty metres apart. Not roughly. Every gap on the approach is the same gap, and the sameness is doing the work: a line of men that regular reads as a fact about the place rather than a decision anyone made.

      Whether they can fight is a question nobody asks, which is the point.

      J.LOT

      A belt formation with nothing in it worth having: no settlement, no licence, nothing to mine.

      What it does have is rock, in quantity, at speed, in a pattern that makes flying through it fast a genuinely stupid idea. The navigational schedules carry a standing advisory against powered transit at speed.

      It appears in the Guard's disciplinary returns eighty-eight times in eleven years, always as the location, always in a charge about unauthorised use of a vessel. Young pilots have been doing this for as long as there have been young pilots.

      Jax Sheel

      The pilot. Officially one of twelve attached to the platoon. In practice, when Castle Team goes anywhere, Jax flies them.

      Wavy raven-black hair and a thick, well-kept moustache that has no business on a face that young. The Guard runs clean-shaven almost everywhere, exemptions take months of argument, and his was simply never challenged. It is a small, cheerful act of not conforming and it suits him completely.

      He came into the team through Yake, trains with the twelve, and drinks with the five. Nobody has ever formally decided he is a member of Castle Team and everybody treats him as one.

      Steady in the air and warm on the ground. He is the one who talks, without making it heavy, about having been pulled out of his own lowest patch by people who bothered.

      Jimzon Cavaris

      also: Jim · Jimzy · Jimz · Jimzo · Jimbo · Jimmy

      Twenty-six. Spec Ops Staff Sergeant, and the man the rest of Castle Team follows without anyone ever having decided that.

      Short brown hair. Stubble he never quite gets on top of. He thinks he looks like nobody in particular, and he is wrong about how much that is true.

      Two marks he cannot walk past a mirror without finding. His nose was broken in a fistfight that got away from everybody and set crooked, because nobody thought to have it fixed. There is a thin burn line across his left cheek where the hair does not grow, from too much to drink, a handful of fireworks and the certainty of being twenty and finished with the Academy. Nobody else notices either one.

      His armour is black and deliberately unshined, with a blue visor. He paints it himself, by hand, every time.

      He wears glasses some of the time, and there is no pattern to when.

      Everyone who likes him has a different name for him, and none of them agreed on one. Calsco Fritt calls him something else entirely, on purpose, and waits every single time for the correction that never comes.

      A promotion to Captain is sitting on somebody's desk. He failed officer school once already, years ago, and has not mentioned that in a while.

      Where he is from, and where he is from

      Born on Modanick and has never once set foot on it. What he knows about his own birthworld is a bedtime story his mother told him: always warm, always daytime, trees taller than houses. She was describing a place she had loved as a student to a boy sitting on a rock, and she made it better than it is.

      He grew up on the Corefuel colony in the wreckage of Wake, where his father ran the station. The family was two months from moving to Creta.

      What he carries

      A grey stone he picked up on the colony road when he was eight. He has had it for twenty years and it is smooth because he rubs it. His mother's service pistol, cleaned since he was old enough to be shown how. A gold holowatch, a gift from a general, shined and with an audible tick to it. An engagement ring in a velvet box that has not been opened in front of anybody.

      What he is like

      Impulsive to the point of recklessness, and funnier in private than anyone outside the team would believe. Table impressions. A napkin moustache. A microwave that went out of a window. He reads his own silence as steadiness and does not notice that everyone around him reads it as absence.

      He is casually bigoted about non-humans in the ordinary, unexamined way of somebody raised where he was raised, and he is unthinkingly kind to children, and he would be embarrassed to have either one pointed out.

      He also uses Crag the way everyone he grew up with uses it, and thinks nothing about it at all.

      Johnny Plasma

      The man who founded the Guard, who never existed.

      The story: after the war, one man with no rank and no property walked from world to world settling quarrels, facing down warlords, teaching people how to keep order, and moving on without taking payment. He founded the Guard and refused every office in it. In most versions he is still out there walking.

      Nobody believes it

      Not the children who are taught it, not the instructors teaching it. Everybody knows. It is in the standard curriculum at two points and it is universal across the member worlds anyway.

      Why bother

      Because the alternative is the incorporation instrument, which survives, and names nine actual founders: four generals of armies that no longer existed and five men with money in shipping, insurance and salvage.

      A founding myth makes you a nation. That document makes you a company.

      Karagash

      A Gashi bounty hunter, and the most reasonably priced frightening thing in the sector.

      Seven feet. Strong through the shoulders and the arms without any of the bulk that usually comes attached, so the size does not register properly until he is standing next to something you know the height of. His hand closes on a wrist like a vise closing, and he is fast in a way that people who have watched it are not able to describe afterwards without their voice changing.

      The face

      He wears a mask across the lower half of it, a breathing apparatus rather than a disguise, and it has been there long enough that the shape of him without it is not a thing many people have seen. Above it, gold and black eyes with no pupil anybody has ever managed to find. You can tell exactly when he looks at something, because the light comes off them differently when they move.

      The rest

      Black suits, cut for a human frame and made to fit his, and he wears them well. A bandolier across the chest, which is not strictly necessary and is clearly a thing he enjoys. And ginger hair, deep and well combed and frankly gorgeous, which on a Gashi is normal and on a seven-foot masked man in a black suit is the detail people bring up first.

      The work

      He hunts for hire. He is extremely good at it and he does not extend mercy, and he is also not angry, ever, about any part of it. The two usually travel together and in him they simply do not. He takes the job, states the price, does the job, collects, and wishes you a good one.

      Nobody knows why he went into this line rather than one of the ten thousand respectable ones a Gashi is expected to want. There is speculation and none of it is worth repeating. The likeliest answer is the one that never gets proposed, which is that he tried it and liked it.

      He is, for what it is worth, modestly priced.

      Katanzaria

      Stone terraces, long tables, wine, and a monumental architecture raised on foundations nobody here laid. Governed by chieftains. Insists, officially and generally, that its people did not come from Wake.

      The disagreement

      Katanzaria holds that its people grew here and are related to nobody. The pre-war genetic surveys we hold in summary place them inside the human range with no distinguishing marker at all. Both are printed. They cannot both be right.

      There is a complication, and it is not a resolution. Katanzaria does have ruins older than its settlement, built in a way its own masons did not use and cannot copy, and a great deal of what stands here stands on them. That the ruins are not human is established. That the people are not human is not.

      Honour, which is not a decoration

      What is said about you after you die is the working currency of public life here, and the world's institutions are shaped around that. Katanzaria keeps the most complete civil registry in this archive, running eleven centuries, because a name is an asset and assets are recorded.

      Succession

      Chieftains, not kings. A title passes within a family but not by birth order: a brother, a cousin or a nephew may take it, and the recorded test is whether the family will be provided for. Alongside the martial component there is an electoral one, and titles have demonstrably moved by each.

      Duelling

      Recognised in statute, restricted by it, and much rarer in the record than in conversation. Twenty-two registered in the last century. Informants describe considerably more.

      Kaz

      A bounty hunter, and a voice giving orders in a room the record does not describe.

      The trade he is in is an old one and a legal one in most of the places it operates, which is why it has stayed as big as it has. Somebody wants a person found, the price is agreed, and no part of the arrangement requires anybody to explain themselves to a government. There are Guard warrants that get worked this way. There are also plenty that do not.

      Of Kaz specifically there is very little: no world, no species, no description, no list of jobs. He works with at least one other person, whom he addresses by name and does not appear to entirely trust.

      Kelsadria Vot Feentor-Jayzin

      goes by: Kelsa

      A pilot with Nova Squadron, and the most organised person in any room she is in.

      Pale blonde, worn up in a bun nearly always. Very fit, in the unremarkable way of somebody who does the work and does not discuss it. Striking eyes, and they are never idle: there is always something going on behind them, and it usually arrives on her face a second before she decides whether to say it.

      She reads stern for about a minute. She is not. She laughs softly and easily once she has decided you are worth the trouble, and after that she is one of the most expressive people on the flight line.

      The hair comes down almost never. Underneath, behind the ears, it is dyed a soft light purple, and there is no version of a duty day in which anybody sees it.

      Royal blood, thinly. House Feentor, Jayzin line, which is the kind of descent half the galaxy can claim: it comes with a seat, a small maintenance, and no money worth the name. She has never drawn either.

      Sansvor

      She grew up in a beautiful ruin. Gaslamp streets, cathedrals and libraries still standing with the roofs open to the sky, museums nobody catalogues, art nobody looks at, and weather coming in through the gaps. She went to school in something like a bombed-out palace with eight other children in it. The teachers were good. The building was losing.

      Every adult around her had a theory about what the world should become. None of them had a roof.

      So she wanted a roof. She heard a teacher had flown in the war, got her licence, and joined the Guard for a pension and citizenship for her family on a world where things get fixed. Not patriotism. Arithmetic.

      How she works

      She dumps her shots on the floor at the bar and pulls the disgusted face along with everybody else. She sings karaoke under protest and then sings it properly.Disciplined, methodical, always with a plan and a fallback. The exact inverse of the man she was going to marry, which is why it worked when it worked: she kept him from flying off the handle and he got her out of her own head. When it stopped working, his unpredictability left her with nothing to stand on and her need to know what came next started to feel like pressure.

      She said it out loud once, testing how it sounded: Kelsa Cavaris. I like the sound of that. He never gave her the ring. It is still in the box.

      Her enlistment ends within the year.

      Kelton

      One city on the whole world, and beyond it small towns and a great deal of empty ground. Nothing edible is produced here.

      What the city makes is the promise that a harvest will be bought, stored, insured and delivered, and the paperwork that makes the promise enforceable. The exchange, the seed registry, the water allocation office, the quarantine authority, forty-one embassies and every insurer writing agricultural risk in the system are all inside it.

      Crop laboratories

      1,188 registered variant lines, developed here rather than on the worlds that grow them. Licence revenue for GC 4461: 96,440,200 credits.

      The arrangement

      A farmer on Weton may plant what she likes, harvest it, and sell it. Water, seed, storage, milling, shipping and sale each require an instrument issued in this city.

      Kelton City

      The only city in the breadbasket, on the only world in it that grows nothing.

      Everything that decides what happens to the food is in here: the exchange, the harvest ledger, the licensing office, the seed registry, the water allocation desk, quarantine, the port, the crop laboratories, forty-one embassies, and every insurer writing agricultural risk in the system.

      It is a city of offices in the middle of a planet of empty ground, and it clears twenty-one billion credits a year without a field anywhere inside the municipal boundary.

      King Matthew

      The reigning King of the Royal systems, and the man giving the address at the Queen's Anniversary for the fourth year running.

      He holds the ordinary powers of the crown, and one that is not ordinary at all. He alone can proclaim an emergency under the High Emergency Council Act, and on that proclamation everything the crown and parliament hold passes to the High Council sitting on Maldo.

      The Act says how the powers go across. It does not say for how long, how they come back, or who reviews it. This has been raised in parliament four times and amended none.

      It has never been invoked.

      Kitalia

      They saw the water coming and they built above it. Pylons driven two kilometres to the seabed, and cities standing on top of them, and no land in use anywhere on the world.

      The engineering

      A glacial melt they could see coming two centuries out, and an answer that worked. This is the most completely documented infrastructure in the archive, because the works were financed from offworld and the financiers wanted certification at every stage: seabed surveys, weld schedules, inspection intervals, unit costs, all of it.

      Foundations run 1,180 to 2,340 metres. Design load 4.1 million tonnes. Certified to 260 knots sustained. They are, by every measure we can apply, magnificent.

      Living on one

      Dense and vertical, because there is no outward. The platform is the civic unit: your roll, your rate, your school, your council. There is no countryside and no farming of any consequence, and the whole arrangement rests on the assumption that the structure holds.

      Population by platform

      Not filed anywhere. Each platform kept its own roll, on itself.

      Burial

      There is no ground. What Kitalians do instead is done over water, and is catalogued separately.

      The Kitalia Platform Collapse

      Loss of one platform city, Kitalia, GC 4461. The structure entered the water. It was not recovered and has not been raised.

      The structure

      INTACT. Commissioned GC 4388. Foundation depth 1,610 metres across 214 pylons. Design load 4.1 million tonnes. Certified storm tolerance 260 knots sustained. Last full inspection GC 4459, passed without qualification. Construction cost 1,204,000,000 credits. Insured value at loss 1,411,000,000 credits, settled in full.

      Cause

      Charges at the pylon heads, placed by cells operating on the world. The Guard investigated, identified four cells, and cleared them out. What this archive holds is the summary; the working material behind it was never released, which is ordinary.

      The dead

      Not established. The platform roll was held on the platform.

      The Restoration's estimate is inferred from the structure and not from the population, there being no surviving record of the population. Taking certified residential floor area against the mean occupancy density returned for comparable platforms in the last decennial survey, the figure falls between 9,000 and 26,000 persons. We publish the method with the number because the number is a guess.

      There is no rubble field. There are no recovered remains. The register of missing persons compiled by the surviving platform administrations is open and is still receiving entries.

      [Compiler's note: we can tell you what the structure cost to the credit. We cannot tell you how many people were standing on it.]

      Korjin Cavaris

      Chemist, engineer, and the man who worked out how to turn the core of a dead planet into fuel.

      He invented the Corefuel synthesis process. Everything that flies, anywhere, runs on the back of what he did in a workshop on a rock, and the licence was signed over to the Guard for a consideration of one credit.

      He ran the extraction station in the Wake field himself. He knew everyone on the colony, he called them by name, and he worked the same hours they did.

      What he was like at the end

      Triumphant. He hit quota, called the entire settlement off work, and ordered a festival for two days later. He had a wife he was plainly still delighted by and two sons, one of whom did not live past five.

      His younger boy asked him, that night, for a spaceship. He did not hesitate for even a moment.

      "Even a spaceship. We're gonna get you one."

      His contract paid on completion of the full year's quota and not a tonne before, which is how these contracts are always written.

      The family was two months from moving to Creta.

      Kraskor

      Big, horned, herd animals on Maspin, with a strong preference for charging first.

      They are herded across the settled belt by people made of smoke, which is a sight visitors do not forget, and they are one of the few things this world produces in enough quantity to sell offworld. Four hundred thousand head a year go out live.

      The Maspin do not eat them in the form they sell them. What they eat is fermented, and it takes years.

      Liles Ninzin

      Somewhere between forty-five and fifty. A general long enough to be respected, and now the one seat on the Guard's Board of Directors that is not a commercial interest.

      He is the man who lifted the floorboard

      He was on the patrol that reached the Wake colony after the raid, and he found a boy under his mother's body when everyone else had written the settlement off.

      He and his then-girlfriend took the child in. They were barely out of college and doing what they could for someone with nowhere else to go. There was an eighth birthday with a small cake, a cheap dinner, and laughter that felt borrowed and was meant kindly.

      They were always kind, and the kindness is what made the distance worse.

      Now

      He runs interference for Jimzon constantly and cannot say why in those words. He offers him a captaincy, quarters, a ship of his own. He refuses to authorise the hunt for the Nhaths, and then authorises it anyway, off the books, with leave time and no paper trail: I don't need proof that I gave this the OK.

      He notices things. The bottom row of a man's medals in the wrong order, at a glance, across a room.

      He is old enough now that his knees are a running joke between the two of them, and old enough to get nostalgic about the Battle of Rudcuff without noticing he is doing it, in the specific way of a man remembering the last time his job was simple.

      What he says he wants, delivered like warmth:

      "One day I'd like us both to be on the Director Board, together, away from the mess of combat."

      He is on a board of seven where every member can be removed by the other six, and where nobody's dissent has ever been written down.

      The little girl in the waiting room

      A child in the medbay at Base Delta, with a puzzle in her lap, waiting for her father.

      She looks up at whoever comes in, blinks, tilts her head, and crosses the room with the kind of confidence only children and fools have. Then she sits down opposite you, uninvited, and starts.

      "Are you a clown?"

      She is a hard audience. Told a joke, she does not laugh. Shown a costume flower that honks twice, she does not laugh at that either. Her mouth holds a perfect little frown.

      Then she explains why she is there.

      "My teacher told me my daddy lost his leg. He isn't here yet. My teacher said he walked on a mine." "Mommy was too."

      Her father is a Trailblazer who stepped on a mine. Her mother was one.

      "Daddy really likes his legs. I think he's probably sad now."

      She will laugh, eventually, at a bad enough joke. How much do rainbows weigh? Not much, they are actually pretty light.

      "I will, mister. You're a funny clown."

      We do not have her name. We are not looking for it.

      Maldo

      They did not build the capital on a beautiful world. They built it on a used-up one, out of the used-up world itself, and every ministry and monument here is made of the ground it stands on.

      Five lives

      An ordinary green world. Then ore, and a boom. Then a century of heavy industry that made the surface uninhabitable and the sky a colour people still describe. Then the ore ran out and everyone left. Then the crown arrived, because a ruin is free land and the material was already lying on site.

      The city

      Built in a documented order, and the building registers survive complete for all sixty-one years of it: capital, then parliament, then monuments, then embassies, then houses spreading outward from all four. 3,308 principal structures.

      The catch

      All of it is Maldo steel, and there is no more Maldo steel. The ore body is worked out. Every repair to a Royal building anywhere is made in some other alloy, and the maintenance returns record the difference, structure by structure, as a falling percentage of original material.

      Now

      Population has fallen in each of the last four decennial returns. Working-age people leave; pensioners arrive. The largest single category of registered business on the world is the sale of antiques and reproductions to visitors.

      The capital of a monarchy is a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from.

      Maldo steel

      The metal the Royal systems are made of, and there is no more of it.

      It came out of one world during one industrial century, and it is better than anything now in production: stronger, longer-lived, and with a surface finish that is the reason it got used for statues and railings as well as for beams.

      Then the ore ran out.

      Every palace, ministry, monument, embassy and lamp post the Royals have raised anywhere is built from a material that cannot be made again. Repairs go in with modern alloys that do not match and never will, and every Royal building is tracked as a slowly falling percentage of its original self.

      Knock a wing down and you can rebuild it. You cannot rebuild it out of the same thing.

      Marfeld

      A world that never lost its big animals. Everywhere else hunted them out. Here they are still in the country, in numbers, and everything about how people live on Marfeld follows from that one fact.

      Weather

      Two months of heat that kills, two months of cold that kills, and the turn between them comes fast enough that people plan for it the way other worlds plan for a storm. Nothing grows reliably. The diet was a hunting diet for most of the world's history and the cooking still tastes like one.

      Why the towns are the size they are

      A settlement here has to be big enough to wall and small enough to move, because the predators come through on the season and a wall is a delay, not an answer. No town on Marfeld has ever exceeded forty thousand people. No city has ever existed. Nobody local finds this remarkable.

      What they sell

      Marfeld sells men. They appear in the muster rolls of every army in the surviving record, in every period, listed by name and settlement and rate of pay, because Marfeld has kept that book for eleven centuries and keeps it still. They are contracted as professionals and paid as professionals, and the world is quite clear that this is a trade and not a tragedy.

      Guard recruiters have had a permanent office here since GC 4409. That is three years after the Guard existed and twenty-two before Marfeld joined it.

      The bombing

      Three times. The first took out the surface of half the northern continent during the war, and no target assessment held by this archive lists Marfeld in that sector at all. The second and third are catalogued as incidental to fighting between other parties.

      Casualty figures for all three exist and disagree with one another by a factor of ten.

      They rebuilt each time. Their own account of it is not grief and not defiance. It is closer to the way another world would talk about a bad winter.

      [Compiler's note: we asked forty-one men from this world to describe the trial. Every one of them declined. Two apologised.]

      The Marfeld beard

      On Marfeld they say hair remembers.

      The beard starts growing during the trial, because a boy out there has no way to stop it. When he comes back it is his, and what it is is a measurement: how long he was out, written on his face by his own body while it was happening.

      You may trim it, shape it, braid it, dye it. Men do all of those and take real care over it.

      You do not shave. Shaving is not a haircut on Marfeld and it is not a fashion choice. It is the renunciation of your family and your bloodline, and there is no lesser version of it. There is nothing in between.

      Which is why Marfeld men in foreign service spend months arguing with grooming regulations rather than pick up a razor, and why a Marfeld man who is clean-shaven has either done something enormous or is not who he says he is.

      One complication

      The Royal court requires its household and its blood to go clean-shaven, by long ceremonial rule. Nobody has ever reconciled the two.
