      The Targath magnetic web

      A construction attributed to the Targath, placed beneath a planetary crust, generating a field of great strength across a wide area.

      The account

      A fleet made planetfall over ground beneath which the web had been laid. The field drew down armour, weapons and personnel. No part of the force withdrew and no member of it survived.

      Status of the account

      It originates within the Guard officer corps and is repeated there. The Restoration has traced it to no document and to no named witness. That no one survived is asserted in the same account that describes what happened, and the Restoration is obliged to note that the two statements cannot both be sourced to the same place.

      The material

      1 gap

      Whatever the account is worth, the ore is real. It is mined, principally by custodial labour, at two Guard installations. Extraction returns are filed by tonnage. The purpose to which the extracted material is put is not filed. [FILING INCOMPLETE]

      Torres Delprest

      Forty-five, and the oldest pilot on Nova Squadron by more than a decade.

      Nova 01 Actual. When the squadron speaks with one voice on the net, it is his.

      He has more hours than anyone on the roster and a posting list that reads like a tour of everywhere the Guard has been. He is still flying, which at his age is unusual and slightly stubborn.

      He is the squadron's centre of gravity: the one who notices when somebody is quiet, who knows which forms exist and what they are actually worth, and who has read the entitlements nobody else has read. If a pilot needs to know how leave works, or what happens to seniority when you stop flying for a while, Torres is who they ask.

      He is also, when it comes to it, gently hurt to find something out by watching rather than being told.Off duty he sings old Backwater country, all of it, badly and with total commitment, and nobody has ever asked him to stop.

      Tracineim

      The faith of the divine feminine, and the state religion of the Royal systems.

      Tracine is the generative principle. Trees are feminine. Worlds are feminine. Water, growth, anything that brings life. The universe itself is read as feminine, and the faith is not much interested in telling you how to behave. It has no code and no list of sins.

      It started at the bottom

      The oldest outside references to it are contemptuous: a religion for slaves, women and children. Then warrior cultures picked it up, and then it became respectable, and then it became the establishment, which is a road several faiths in this volume have walked.

      How it is actually practised

      Barely, and constantly. There is no weekly assembly, no obligation, and no clergy in the way other faiths have clergy. What there is, is a blessing people say when they part:

      May Traceen be with you.

      Said by the devout, said by people who have not thought about it in years, and said by soldiers who would tell you flatly they believe none of it.

      The Queen

      She is not held to be immortal. The crown never claimed she could not die. It claimed she is Tracine's presence on Shayron, which is not a lifespan. It is a tenure.

      Trailblazer Base Delta

      A Trailblazer port on Maspin, built up into the trees.

      Bungalows on stilts and platforms, woven rugs, ferns everywhere, lanterns strung between branches, and the Elder Tree going up out of sight beyond the edge of it. There is a medbay with two theatres, a machine shop, and ground for four medium hulls. Flooms are kept in the surrounding district and largely do as they please.

      No walls

      No perimeter, no watchtowers, no emplacements, no guards. This is true of every Trailblazer installation and it is deliberate: they are guests on somebody's world and they build like guests. Soldiers who see it for the first time tend to describe it as a trap someone forgot to set.

      Maspin work here at every grade, including running things, which is not the arrangement anywhere else on this world.

      The Trailblazer doctor

      The surgeon at Base Delta. Wears a smug little smirk almost permanently, gives you the bad news fast and flat, and then softens once it has landed.

      He is the one who explains floomicide to families: very effective, in very short supply, and it costs you your grip on reality for as long as the healing takes.

      Why he believes in shamans

      He will pull down his collar and show you the scar, a large burned circle in the middle of his chest. A kraskor stampede, while they were clearing ground for a helipad. The horn went through his chest and into his heart.

      "My mates told me the shaman ran over, murmured strange words, and somehow stopped me from bleeding out. They say he paused my dying body. Animated my legs just long enough to walk back to the car. Then hooked me up to floomicide. Call it magic or whatever you want. But it saved me."

      A man of medicine who takes the local mysticism entirely seriously, because it restarted him.

      Trailblazer Logistics

      Operating arm of the Trailblazers. Sectioned by function.

      Sections are numbered and are filed with the concession authority of each world in which they operate. Recorded sections include survey and seismic elevation, port construction, freight handling, medical, and salvage recovery.

      Section personnel work on contract to the section and not to the world, which places them outside local labour registers. The arrangement is noted in three concession instruments and objected to in none.

      The Trailblazers

      Soldiers from both sides of a war nobody won, building ports for worlds the shipping lanes forgot. Grey coveralls, orange trim, and a shovel on the badge.

      Who they are

      Veterans of the Autumnal party and of C.O.R.D., in proportions the body does not record because its founding instrument states that prior service is not a matter for enquiry. As far as we can tell that is actually observed.

      What they do

      The war cut the lanes and whole sectors went dark. The Guard holds a monopoly on the little that still moves. The Trailblazers reopen the routes, build the port where none survived, and run it under concession: fixed term, revenue split with the local council, paid for in land and housing.

      They are the only organised logistics network in the settled galaxy operating outside Guard control, and they got there by dealing with local councils rather than with the Guard at all.

      What it cost them

      The founding accounts are held. The body ran at a loss for eleven years and its people went unpaid for seven of them. The arrears schedule is filed. It was settled in full in GC 4443.

      No walls

      Every Trailblazer installation in the concession filings has no perimeter, no watchtower, no emplacement and no armed establishment. We checked this against the construction schedules, which list no such item, and against three informants, who confirmed it with some amusement.

      Standing

      They hold seats on local councils on at least four worlds, in every case by the council's own instrument and not by any treaty.

      Translator chips

      A Guard-made implant that puts Galactic Standard in your head. It goes in at the neck.

      One of the very few things the galaxy has managed to start manufacturing again since the Wipe, which makes it a small triumph and a very profitable line. Guard personnel get one if the job needs it. Everybody else buys one, and they are not cheap.

      Each unit is serialised, and the serial ranges are allocated by production quarter, which means any chip anyone finds can be dated to within three months of when it was made.

      The scar

      The placement leaves a mark, and the surgical notes say so plainly: it is unavoidable at that position. The same notes mention, without further comment, that some patients ask for the implant specifically because there is already something at their neck they would rather people did not look at.

      Vance

      A man who will argue with you about what is true, and will not raise his voice while he does it.

      He has a position and it is not a complicated one: that being right is a smaller thing than being honest, and that most people who are pleased with how clever they are have quietly stopped doing the harder of the two. He puts it plainly, without ornament, and he puts it the same way the fourth time as the first.

      Why it lands badly

      Because he is unbothered. The person opposite him gets angrier as it goes and he does not move, and there is nothing more infuriating than a man who is not competing. Called weak for it, he takes that as a description rather than an insult and continues.

      Vando

      A Trailblazer, and the reason the Yinmelon story gets told at least once a rotation.

      The run works like this. You put in at small settlements nobody surveys twice, and you sell what people at small settlements actually want: rockroot by the sack, glazberries, spice bundles tied with string. All of it real. All of it worth what you charge.

      The fragmentation grenades ride in the Yinmelon sauce cans. Yinmelon sauce is thick, sweet, faintly orange, and sold in a can heavy enough that nobody picks one up expecting it to be light.

      The one time it nearly came apart was a farmer's market on Monver, where a guard who had been standing in the sun for six hours asked for a taste.

      He lost a thumb.

      Vando tells it as a comedy, and it mostly is, and everybody laughs at the same place every time.

      The Vitula

      Two metres and more. Grey, and wet to the touch. Eight white eyes set around the head, so that there is no direction they cannot see. On the back, folded and useless, a pair of wings that have not carried anything in a very long time.

      The body

      Insect-descended, and without the shell you would expect from that: all of the mass is muscle and nerve. They breathe badly off their own worlds and wear masks everywhere else, bought by the employer and deducted from the wage.

      Pain registers in them below the human mean. That is a property of the nervous system, documented in the pre-war literature, and it means what it says: they feel it less, so they keep working.

      The disagreement

      Guard instructional material says the Vitula have a collective mind and no individual will. The surviving biology says pheromone signalling, proximity awareness, and a distress sense good to about 1.6 kilometres that carries no content beyond the fact that somebody is hurt.

      Both are printed here. They describe different animals.

      Work

      Excavation, tunnelling, deep foundation, haulage, foundry, and armed contract. Vitula crews appear in the construction record of eleven worlds, including as subcontractors on the Kitalia pylons, listed by crew and by rate. The kingdoms themselves are small, farmed at the surface and mined underneath.

      When a king or queen dies, the pattern in the record is not succession crisis and not reprisal. It is a cluster of new engagements. The crews go and find whoever is hiring. This has been observed four times.

      One further fact

      Guard field instruction includes anatomy for this people, specifying the location of the heart. The manual is INTACT, is in current issue, and places that lesson at the same point in the syllabus as the lesson on how to operate a weapon.

      Wake

      also known as: Waketin · the Wakeful Islands · Origin

      A field of rock where a planet used to be. Held almost everywhere to be where humans came from, on the strength of genetic sampling whose method did not survive the people who used it.

      Before

      Every source we hold agrees it was a capital world. That is the only detail about this planet on which our sources do not disagree.

      There is no census material. No municipal roll, no tax register, no conscription list, no birth record, nothing. Several people have described the census offices to us by location. None of the buildings survive.

      The loss

      Guard records say one ordnance deployment, Autumnal forces, GC 4394, over in under an hour.

      Thirty-eight people across eleven settlements say it took between two and nine days. Six of them describe the sky changing colour before anything was heard. Four describe evacuation orders. One describes those orders being countermanded.

      We print both. They cannot both be correct.

      After

      Mantle and core in pieces, sixty-one of them dense enough to be worth working. The Corefuel comes out of those, and it comes out of nowhere else with a licence on it, and the licence is issued by the Guard Board of Directors alone.

      The ledgers for that trade are INTACT and unusually complete. Licensed extraction for GC 4461: 812,443.6 standard tonnes.

      People lived out there while it was worked. Houses on the larger fragments, held down and given air by spires burning the planet they were standing on. There was a school.

      Settlement names, populations and outcomes were not filed.

      [Compiler's note: we hold four hundred and eleven pages of extraction ledger for this world and one page of anything else.]

      Wake Extraction Station

      The works where the homeworld gets turned into fuel. In the paperwork it is called Station, without a qualifier, because there is only one.

      Raw fragment material comes in, synthesis happens, and certified Corefuel goes out to Guard transports. Everything that flies anywhere begins here.

      The quota

      The Board sets a number each year and the station meets it. The contract pays on certification of the full year's quota and not before, which means a station chief spends every year working toward a single date. Miss it and the year pays nothing.

      The final year on record came in at 443.6 tonnes over.

      Class 2

      That rating entitles the station to point-defence parts every quarter, on request. The entitlements are all on file. The delivery notes are kept somewhere else and that series has gaps in it.

      The Wakeful Islands

      What people called the rocks they lived on. It is not a filing term. We use it because they use it, and because no document we hold has a name for the inhabited part of a dead planet.

      How many

      Sixty-one fragments are catalogued as worth extracting from. Some unstated number of those carried people. Our estimate of nine to thirty comes from counting gravity spire installations on the parts requisitions, and should be treated as exactly that good.

      Why nobody was counted

      They lived there under an extraction licence, not a settlement charter. In law they were not colonists. There was therefore no settlement roll to be on, which is how a place with a school ends up with no population figure.

      What it was like, from testimony: houses linked by intercom because there was no network to link them with. One landing pad a fragment, one supply run a week. Gardens under spire air. And twice a standard year, for several days, an orbital condition that took the radio out entirely and against which the only remedy was to work to the published timetable.

      Weton

      Grain from one horizon to the other, worked by families on long instruments with machinery nobody can build any more.

      Harvest, GC 4461

      1,204,880,600 tonnes, of which 1,204,880,600 tonnes were bought at the scheduled price. The purchase guarantee has been met in every year on record.

      What Weton does not have

      Its soil comes from Sheel. Its water is allocated from Corr. Its seed is licensed from Tall. Its grain leaves raw and is milled on Dorrow. It holds none of those functions and has never asked for one.

      The machines

      Every combine and hauler here is pre-war and irreplaceable, kept running under the system repair entitlement by yards whose senior mechanics are the most consequential people in any given district. A farmer here can afford to fix the tractor. That is not true anywhere else in this archive and everybody here knows it.

      Wages are good. Wages are in scrip.

      Wingsuits

      Personal atmospheric descent equipment. Permits controlled entry to a surface from a vessel in atmosphere without a landing.

      In current manufacture and in general service. The equipment is simple, the materials are producible, and the loss returns record failure rates that the Guard's own safety schedule describes as within tolerance and does not otherwise characterise.

      Employment in weather is governed by a standing order which sets limits and provides for those limits to be exceeded on the authority of the officer commanding.

      Reader's key

      Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 9.

      The Wipe

      vernacular: the Fry

      In GC 4401 every computer in the galaxy stopped, and everything any of them was holding stopped with it. Paper survived. That is the entire reason this volume exists.

      The formal word is the Wipe, and it is what the filings and the law use. Everybody who was actually there calls it the Fry.

      How complete

      Total, as far as anything we can check. In nineteen years nobody on any world has described to us a device that kept working, and no archive anywhere has reported a surviving data holding. We keep the request open.

      What went with it
      • every network. Communication fell back to couriers, unamplified radio, and towers the churches owned
      • every account. Money became paper, then became an entry in a Guard ledger
      • every drone and every unmanned system. Saigo is still trying to rebuild them
      • every navigational archive. The lanes were re-surveyed by hand over thirty years, and the survey authority publishes what that cost in ships and crews
      • the census

      What survived

      Insurers, port authorities, tax offices, monasteries and shipping clerks, all of whom kept duplicates in cabinets because that was the procedure. By weight this archive is about eighty per cent commercial and administrative paperwork.

      Which is why we can tell you the tonnage of a cargo that left a world sixty years ago and not how many people were living on it.

      [Compiler's note: the Guard's accounting division is understood to have retyped twenty years of ledger by hand after the event. We have applied four times to see it and have received three acknowledgements.]

      Yakib Yalitio

      goes by: Yake

      Castle Team's medic, and the only one of them who does arithmetic before agreeing to something.

      Evenly tanned, because he spends his rest days outside while everyone else is in the bar. Sandy brown hair that falls across his forehead the moment the helmet comes off. An easy, unbothered face that has nothing to do with how he actually works, which is fast and cold and very good. Yellow visor.

      Home

      A world he does not talk up much, with one thing on it worth the trip: a starship wreck the size of a city, Maldo era, so thoroughly overgrown that people climb it like a mountain. He climbed it with his father as a boy, in magboots, which were later killed by a lightning storm and never replaced.

      Faith

      He was raised religious in a way that is mostly relaxed and has a few strange corners he does not explain to outsiders. When he filled in the form that asks a recruit what rites they want, the list of eighty-eight faiths did not have his on it, so he wrote it in himself.

      Money

      He sends most of his pay home and has done since the day he signed. He is not shy about why, and he does not dress it up:

      "I've fought next to you on every battle, but I will put my life on the line before my career. If I die, my family gets paid."

      He is not the coward of this group. He is the only one keeping score.

      Yinmelon

      A big, heavy, fleshy fruit, mostly processed into a sauce of the same name and shipped in sealed tins by the container load.

      It is one of the highest-volume food items moving anywhere, which is exactly why it is also one of the most common things written on the outside of a container holding something else entirely. Customs seizure returns are full of Yinmelon sauce that is not Yinmelon sauce.

      The sauce itself is decent. Somebody has a story about a guard at a farmer's market on Monver who took a bribe in the form of a taste and lost a thumb to what was in the tin.
